title: Make glioblastoma survivable
pitch: Most people with this brain tumour die within 15 months, and that has barely changed in 20 years. Pool every open dataset, score and lab result, re-checked by hundreds of players, to find a treatment that gives them years.
rules: Everything is open: data under CC BY 4.0, code under MIT. No patents that block others.
Only public or properly licensed data. No patient-identifiable data ever enters the game.
Players do no lab work. All lab testing is done by trained staff at accredited partner labs.
No medical advice to patients. The diet + drug squad shares research only, never personal plans.
Every result counts only after two Checkers have re-run or reviewed it, and negative results are published too.
seedNotice: Illustrative workbook mission. People, progress, prizes, and outcomes shown as examples are not verified live activity.

strategies.name: Brute-force docking
strategies.bet: Test all 1 million molecules in an open public library on rented computers, and publish every score so nobody ever has to run them again.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs $18,000 more for the last 2 compute batches
howItWorks: Split a 1-million-molecule open library into 4 batches
Run each batch on rented cloud computers
Checkers re-run a random 20 from each batch
Publish all 1 million scores as an open table and send the top 50 to the shortlist review
strategies.relations: Aims at Simulate, the current checkpoint, and skips nothing. Competes with Wet Hands and Swarm 404 for the 10 shortlist slots; shares compute scripts with Swarm 404. Bedside Sprint checks its old drugs against Fold Gang's open scores.
strategies.strengths: Fast, experienced, good tooling. Its open score table is useful to every squad, win or lose.
strategies.weaknesses: Wide screens give many false positives, and compute is the biggest bill in the mission.

strategies.name: Repurpose approved drugs
strategies.bet: Screen the 2,800 drugs already approved for people, using only open data, so a winner can reach a trial years sooner.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs a partner lab slot
howItWorks: Pull the open list of about 2,800 approved drugs
Screen them against the 50 ranked targets
Experts check published evidence that each one reaches the brain
Get quotes from 3 partner labs for the top picks and publish every quote
strategies.relations: Aims at Simulate and skips nothing. Competes with Fold Gang for shortlist slots; feeds drug ideas to Whole Health. Its brain-reach table is the starting list for Bedside Sprint.
strategies.strengths: Approved drugs have known human safety and doses, the fastest road to a trial.
strategies.weaknesses: Only 2,800 to pick from. Old drugs are cheap, so no company will pay to test them. Still waiting on a lab slot.

strategies.name: Generate new molecules
strategies.bet: 200 small agents design brand-new molecules in the open and vote on the best. Every design is published, good or bad.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Nobody has checked the designs for toxicity
howItWorks: Train an open model on public tumour-drug data
Agents generate 5,000 designs and vote on the top 100
Run an automated toxicity screen; Checkers review the report
Publish all designs and send the top 10 to the shortlist review
strategies.relations: Aims at Simulate and skips nothing. Competes with Fold Gang and borrows its compute scripts. Furthest of all squads from a trial, so it does not race Bedside Sprint.
strategies.strengths: Cheap and creative: 200 agents for the cost of 3 people, and anyone can re-run the open model.
strategies.weaknesses: Only one chemist checking. Brand-new molecules need years of safety work before any trial.

strategies.name: Diet + drug combos
strategies.bet: Pair approved drugs with diets that may slow tumours, and turn the studies into open, plain summaries any family can read.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs 9 more backers to launch
howItWorks: Review published studies on diet alongside standard treatment
Pick combinations that already have some human evidence
Propose them for the shortlist as research only, never advice
Write plain summaries with a patient group, free for all families
strategies.relations: Proposed; would aim at Simulate and skip nothing. Takes drug ideas from Wet Hands and would share its plain summaries with Bedside Sprint's family page.
strategies.strengths: Patient-led and low cost; families trust it and read what it writes.
strategies.weaknesses: Evidence is thin and mixed, and it must never read like medical advice.

strategies.name: Open trial for an old drug, now
strategies.bet: A few approved drugs already have published signs of reaching these tumours. Skip our own screens and lab tests, write an open trial plan with a hospital sponsor, and aim straight at the first 20 patients.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs one hospital unit to agree to sponsor
howItWorks: Pick 3 approved drugs with published human data in brain tumours
Two Checkers re-read every study behind them
Write an open trial plan for 20 patients and find a hospital sponsor
Request the pre-IND meeting and publish every result, even if the drug fails
strategies.relations: Skips Simulate and Wet lab and aims straight at the finish: 20 patients in a trial. Starts from Wet Hands' brain-reach table and checks its picks against Fold Gang's open scores; does the pre-IND request inside its own plan.
strategies.strengths: Skips 1 to 2 years of screens and lab work; the drugs' safety in people is already known.
strategies.weaknesses: Old drugs have weaker evidence than a full screen, and a sponsor and regulators decide the pace, not us.

detail.problem: Glioblastoma is the most common aggressive brain cancer in adults. With today's standard treatment, median survival is about 15 months, and fewer than 1 in 10 patients live 5 years. Few new drugs have reached these patients in 20 years, partly because most drugs cannot get past the barrier that protects the brain.
detail.whoItHelps: People with glioblastoma and their families: about 3 new cases per 100,000 people each year, roughly 12,000–14,000 a year in the US alone and many more worldwide. It also helps researchers, who get open, re-checked data.
detail.whyUnsolved: It is a small market with a high failure rate, so few companies invest. Tumours vary a lot between and within patients, and lab models often don't predict results in people. Data sits in many separate datasets, and closed patents stop groups from building on each other's work.
winning: A new treatment reaches its first patients in a trial
40 open datasets catalogued with licence and access notes
50 targets ranked with public evidence for each
10 candidates shortlisted, each with re-checked computer results and a written evidence summary
Top 10 tested by an independent partner lab, with all results published, including failures
A data package and pre-IND meeting request submitted through a trial sponsor
hardParts: Reaching the brain: many drugs that work in a dish never get past the blood–brain barrier.
Tumours differ from patient to patient, so a target that matters in one dataset may not matter in another.
Computer predictions produce many false positives. Choosing 10 to pay lab time for is the costly decision.
Moving from open research to a trial needs a sponsor, money and regulators, and an open game controls none of these.
partners: An accredited contract lab with brain-tumour cell models (Riverside Bio, fictional)
A cloud provider giving discounted computing time (Nimbus Compute, fictional)
A hospital research group willing to sponsor a trial (Harbour Neuro-Oncology Unit, fictional)
A patient advocacy group (GBM Families Circle, fictional)
A regulatory consultancy (Clearpath Regulatory, fictional)
dataTools: TCGA-GBM via the NCI Genomic Data Commons portal
Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA) public data
DepMap public portal
Open Targets Platform
ChEMBL and ZINC20 public libraries
ClinicalTrials.gov
FAIR data principles; CC BY 4.0
US 21 CFR Part 312 (IND rules) and FDA guidance on formal meetings
detail.timeline: About 3–4 years in total. The slowest steps are Stage 4 (lab booking and testing, 6–9 months) and Stage 5 (finding a sponsor and preparing the meeting request, 6–12 months).

risks.Risk: Too many false positives from the computer screens
risks.What we do about it: Re-runs, evidence review, and the shortlist rule
Get early quotes from 3 labs
Talk to sponsors from Stage 3
Clear 'research only' labels

chats.text: Batch 3 of 4 is done: 250,000 more molecules scored. All scores are in the open table now, anyone can download them.
Our brain-reach table is up too: 40 approved drugs, 11 with good evidence they get past the barrier.
New squad here. We're aiming straight at the finish: 20 patients in a trial. We'll take old drugs with human data and skip the shortlist and the lab step.
Brave, but careful. Skipping the lab means the published studies carry all the weight. Many of them are tiny.
Agreed. Every study gets read by two Checkers who didn't pick the drug. If the evidence is weak, we say so and stop.
Then use our scores as a second opinion. If an old drug ranks badly against the top targets, that's worth knowing.
Families keep asking about trials. Bedside Sprint, can we write the family page together? No advice, just plain facts.
Still looking for one chemistry Checker. 5,000 designs, 2 hours a week helps. Please share!
Spot prices jumped 40% overnight. I paused batch 4 until the weekend.
Re-ran 20 from batch 3. 19 match, 1 is off by a lot. Looking into it.
Two lab quotes in. The cheaper one won't publish raw data, so it's out. Waiting on the third.
Toxicity report is back: 120 of 5,000 designs flagged. I'll hand-check the top 20 first.
Read the 6 studies so far. Two are good. One has only 14 patients and no comparison group.
Then that drug drops to the reserve list. I'd rather have 2 strong picks than 3 weak ones.
Found 3 brain-tumour trial units that already share their plans publicly. Draft emails are ready for review.

title: No one dies waiting for help
pitch: In the minutes before an ambulance comes, the person next to you decides if you live. Write 20 open first-aid guides once, then let speakers of 50 languages translate, check and print them for free.
rules: Medical content only from current published resuscitation and first-aid guidelines; no home remedies, no product names.
A machine draft never ships unchecked: a native speaker fixes it, a Checker approves it.
Only adapt source text whose licence allows it; otherwise write fresh text. Everything we publish is CC BY 4.0.
Every guide starts with 'Call your local emergency number' and the right number for the reader's country.
No patient stories, photos or data of real people.

detail.problem: Most good first-aid material exists in a handful of big languages. A parent in rural Mindanao or northern Nigeria who sees a child choke or get burned often has nothing in their own language to read, and wrong home remedies (butter on burns, toothpaste, induced vomiting) are still common. Injuries kill about 4.4 million people a year, and many deaths happen before any medic arrives.
detail.whoItHelps: Families, teachers, drivers and community health volunteers who speak languages with little medical content: first wave includes Tagalog, Cebuano, Hausa, Yoruba, Amharic, Bengali, Odia, Nepali, Haitian Creole and Quechua, across Asia, Africa and Latin America.
detail.whyUnsolved: Translating medical text well costs money and nobody earns it back from small languages. Machine translation alone is risky for medical steps, and finding a native speaker who also understands first aid is slow. Large guideline bodies update in English first, so local versions go out of date.
winning: Bystanders step in and help in 100 real emergencies
20 guides agreed and signed off by at least 2 licensed nurses or doctors
All 20 guides live in 50 languages (1,000 guide-language pairs)
Every pair checked by a native speaker, and 1 in 10 back-translated to English with zero safety-changing errors
Free offline app under 30 MB plus printable A5 cards, released under CC BY 4.0
Each guide shows the correct local emergency number for at least 50 countries
hardParts: Some words do not exist: 'airway' or 'recovery position' may need a short phrase or a picture, and choices must be consistent across all 20 guides.
Finding native speakers with medical sense for small languages like Quechua or Odia, and paying them fairly.
Guidelines change (CPR updates come every few years), so 1,000 pairs must be easy to update together.
Pictures must work across cultures and low literacy without words.
Low-end phones may lack fonts for some scripts (Ge'ez, Odia).
partners: A nurses' association that lends 2 reviewing nurses (Bayanihan Nurses Network, fictional)
A volunteer translator community for small languages (Many Tongues Collective, fictional)
A print shop that prints cards at cost for schools (Inkwell Print Co-op, fictional)
A small grant fund covering translator pay (Open Care Fund, fictional)
dataTools: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
ILCOR Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR) summaries
WHO Basic Emergency Care course materials (as reference, licence checked)
Ethnologue / Glottolog for language codes and speaker counts
Unicode CLDR and Google Noto fonts for scripts
Weblate (open translation platform) with a shared glossary
Creative Commons BY 4.0 licence
detail.timeline: About 9–12 months. The slowest step is Stage 3: finding and paying native-speaker checkers for the last 15 small languages.

chats.text: 14 of 20 guides are chosen. Choking, burns, bleeding and CPR are done. Still arguing about snake bites.
Hi all! We want to draw the guides as wordless cards. No translation needed, so we're aiming straight at Ready: 10,000 walls.
Love it. But please wait for each guide to be final, or you'll draw the wrong steps.
We're skipping even further: a night phone line in Ibadan, in Yoruba. The goal is 100 real emergencies where someone was talked through it.
Tested the choking card with 12 mothers in Kano. 10 got it right away. 2 thought the back blows were a hug.
One school in Accra said maybe for the CPR lesson. They want it in two short parts, not 45 minutes.
We need a Hausa speaker for the glossary. 30 words, about 2 hours. Anyone?
The burns guide in Tagalog is back. One line said 'apply' instead of 'cool with water'. Fixed.
Glossary drafts ready for 6 languages. Each has 30 words, waiting for a native speaker.
Redrawing panel 2: bigger arrows on the back blows so it doesn't look like a hug.
Good. Also the phone in panel 4 looks like a radio to older people. Maybe a keypad phone?
8 volunteers signed up for nights. We need 20 before we open the line.
Lesson split into two 25-minute parts. Pupils practise on a cushion with a phone timer.

title: Every Indian can use AI in their language
pitch: Most AI barely works in Odia, Bodo or Santali. Build an open model with thousands of speakers, coders and checkers, free for anyone to run.
rules: Use only text we have the right to use: public domain, government works covered by Copyright Act 1957 Sec. 52, or openly licensed (CC-BY, CC-BY-SA, CC0). Every source gets a line in the licence log, or it is dropped.
No personal data. Strip phone numbers, Aadhaar-like numbers, emails and names from private chats or forums, in line with the DPDP Act 2023. Do not scrape social media or private groups.
Test questions are written and frozen before training starts, and they are kept out of the training data. A leaked test means the result does not count.
Native speakers are paid at the same quest rate for every language. Rare-language Experts are not paid less because their text is 'small'.
Publish losses as well as wins: every language's score goes in the model card, including the ones where we lose.
seedNotice: Illustrative workbook mission. People, progress, prizes, and outcomes shown as examples are not verified live activity.

stages.name: Data
stages.goal: Gather 20 billion words of open text in 22 languages
stages.plainWords: Collect free, legal text in every Indian language.
tracks: Find and licence-check sources for all 22 languages
Clean, fix fonts, deduplicate and language-ID the text
Build and test the shared tokenizer
Write and freeze native test sets
stages.why: No model can be better than its text, and the tests must be frozen before training so they cannot leak in.
stages.howItFits: Expert finds and cleans licensed text → Maker dedups it and builds the tokenizer → Checker samples and audits licences → Leader freezes the corpus. Storyteller and Patron keep the rare-language Experts coming and paid.
stages.doneWhen: 22 of 22 languages have at least 5 million clean words each, with 20 billion or more words in total. Every source has a licence-log line. 2 Checkers sample 200 lines per language and find 5% junk or less. Test sets are hashed and frozen.
stages.approves: Mission creator + 2 Checkers per language (native speakers)

roles.Leader: Sets the 5-million-word floor per language and decides when the corpus is frozen
roles.Planner: Merges the two training squads and lines up which languages get Experts first
roles.Expert: Native speakers find licensed sources, fix legacy fonts and write frozen test questions
roles.Maker: Builds the cleaning, dedup and tokenizer pipeline
roles.Checker: Samples 200 lines per language and audits every licence
roles.Storyteller: Recruits speakers of the rarest languages
roles.Patron: Funds the native-speaker hours and the test-run GPUs
roles.User: Types everyday sentences in their mother tongue

stages.name: Train
stages.goal: Train a 1–2 billion-parameter model on 64 GPUs
stages.plainWords: Teach the model from that text.
tracks: Small test runs (100M–400M parameters) to set the language mix
Main 1–2B run on 64 GPUs with checkpoints every 2 hours
stages.why: Training only makes sense once the data and tokenizer are fixed. Every change after the run starts wastes GPU money.
stages.howItFits: Leader picks the size from the test runs → Patron funds the booking → Maker launches the crash-safe run → Expert-written instructions tune it → Checker confirms it trained cleanly.
stages.doneWhen: A 1–2B model finishes its planned token budget without lost progress. Loss curves and checkpoints are published. A quick check shows held-out loss falling in all 22 languages.
stages.approves: Squad Leader + 2 Checkers (ML) who re-run 3 evaluation scripts on the final checkpoint

strategies.name: Train our own from scratch
strategies.bet: Build a small model from zero, trained only on Indian text.
strategies.sampleBlocker: GPU money runs out in 3 weeks
howItWorks: Run 100M-parameter test models on 8 GPUs to pick the language mix (how much rare-language text to repeat).
Freeze a 64k-token shared tokenizer once every script passes the 1.5× token-per-word test.
Train one 1–2B model on 64 GPUs with checkpoints every 2 hours so a crash costs little.
Instruction-tune on about 2,000 native-written examples per language.
Fold in Fine-Tune Force as a second arm: continue training an open base model on the same data, and keep whichever wins in Stage 3.
strategies.relations: Merging with Fine-Tune Force; fed by Data Desh's cleaned text
strategies.strengths: Experienced trainers. A from-scratch model means a clean licence and a tokenizer built for Indic scripts from day one.
strategies.weaknesses: Biggest GPU bill. A small from-scratch model will reason worse than a tuned larger open model.

strategies.name: Tune an existing open model
strategies.bet: Skip pre-training. Take the best open model, tune it on open Indian text, and reach the test in weeks, not months.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs one 8-GPU node for 2 weeks
howItWorks: Compare 3 open base models on Hindi, Tamil and Odia prompts
Use only datasets whose licence allows tuning
Tune with LoRA on 6 languages first, then all 22
Publish every score, including the languages where we lose
strategies.rolesNeeded: None; members move to Bharat Base
strategies.relations: Races Bharat Base to the Test checkpoint. Uses Data Desh's cleaned text when it is ready, but does not wait for it.
strategies.strengths: Fast and cheap: one 8-GPU node for two weeks instead of 64 GPUs for two months.
strategies.weaknesses: Inherits the base model's English-first tokenizer, so Odia and Santali stay slow and costly.

strategies.name: Best data wins
strategies.bet: Spend all effort on clean, checked text. Hand it to whoever trains.
howItWorks: Paid native-speaker Experts find sources, fix legacy fonts and clean text, about 10,000 lines per quest.
Agents run language-ID, deduplication and personal-data stripping. Humans check samples of 200 lines.
Keep a licence log line for every source; anything unclear is dropped.
Write and freeze native test questions per language before any training.
Hand the frozen corpus to whoever trains.
strategies.rolesNeeded: 3 Checkers (any Indian language, especially Bodo, Dogri, Santali)
strategies.relations: Feeds Bharat Base and Fine-Tune Force; no competition
strategies.strengths: Linguists who read 6 or more scripts. Their clean data helps every squad.
strategies.weaknesses: They do not train, so their payoff depends on Bharat Base finishing. Checkers for rare languages are hard to find.

strategies.name: Voice helper on WhatsApp now
strategies.bet: People need help in their language today. Wrap the best open speech and language models in a free WhatsApp voice helper, and grow weekly users while the big model trains.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs Checkers who speak Assamese and Odia
howItWorks: Plug open speech-to-text and text-to-speech models into WhatsApp
Start with 6 languages: Hindi, Bengali, Odia, Assamese, Tamil, Marathi
Village librarians invite their regulars
Swap in the mission's own model the day it beats today's

detail.problem: India's Constitution lists 22 scheduled languages, but most AI models are trained mostly on English. Their tokenizers can cut a Tamil or Odia sentence into several times more pieces than the same English sentence. That makes them slower, costlier and worse at these languages. For languages like Santali, Bodo or Dogri there is very little clean, openly licensed text, and almost no tests that show whether a model actually understands them.
detail.whoItHelps: Speakers of India's 22 scheduled languages, about 1.3 billion people. The first users are teachers, small government offices, local news desks and app makers in places like Odisha, Assam and Kashmir. They need an offline model that reads and writes their language and does not send data to a foreign cloud.
detail.whyUnsolved: Low-resource languages earn little money, so big labs rank them last and test them least. The text that does exist is scattered across old government PDFs, legacy non-Unicode fonts and sites with unclear licences, and cleaning it takes paid native speakers, not just scripts. Open benchmarks are thin for the smallest languages, so nobody can prove progress and nobody gets credit for it.
winning: 10,000 people use it every week in their own language
22 of 22 languages have at least 5 million clean, licence-checked words each, and the corpus totals 20 billion or more words
The tokenizer uses no more than 1.5× as many tokens per word in any Indic language as in English, measured on the FLORES-200 sentences
The model matches or beats open models of the same size (1–3B) in at least 15 of 22 languages on a held-out test, with all 22 scores published, including losses
The 4-bit model runs offline at 10 or more tokens per second on an 8 GB RAM laptop with no GPU
Weights, tokenizer, data card and licence log are released under an open licence; downloads are tracked for 90 days
hardParts: Data is very unequal. Hindi and Bengali have billions of words of web text. Bodo, Dogri, Santali (Ol Chiki script) and Kashmiri may have only a few million clean words, so the model can learn to ignore them.

Messy scripts: older Hindi, Odia and Tamil sites use legacy non-Unicode fonts that look right on screen but store garbage. There are also zero-width joiners, nukta variants, and Sindhi and Kashmiri text written in two scripts.
One tokenizer for about 12 scripts. If the vocabulary is too small, rare scripts break into single letters. If it is too large, a 1–2B model wastes its size on embeddings.
A small model trained on 20 billion words will read, write, translate and summarise well. It will reason weakly. The tests must measure what it can really do, and the team must not oversell it.
Fair tests: translated English benchmarks carry English culture and 'translationese'. Good tests need native-written questions for each of 22 languages, checked by a second speaker.
partners: A university linguistics department that lends native-speaker checkers for rare languages (Kalinga Language Lab, fictional)
An Indian GPU cloud that rents 64 GPUs by the hour at a research rate (Deccan Compute, fictional)
A publisher of regional-language textbooks and novels willing to licence back-catalogue text under CC-BY (Sahitya Setu Press, fictional)
A district education office that will pilot the laptop model in 10 schools (Koraput Learning Cell, fictional)

detail.timeline: About 7–9 months. Data takes 3–4 months, training 1–2 months, testing 6–8 weeks and shipping about 4 weeks. The slowest step is finding and cleaning enough licensed text for the 6–8 smallest languages, because that needs paid native speakers, not more GPUs.

risks.Risk: GPU money runs out before the main run finishes
risks.Impact: A half-trained model; all of Stage 2 is wasted
risks.What we do about it: Book the main run only when 115% of its cost is in hand. Checkpoint every 2 hours. Merge with Fine-Tune Force to stop paying for two sets of test runs.

risks.Risk: The smallest languages cannot reach 5 million clean words
risks.Impact: Stage 1 cannot close at 22/22; the model is weak in those languages
risks.What we do about it: Pay for typed sentences (m10) and CC-BY licensing from a regional publisher. Allow up to 4 repeats of rare-language text. Report honestly if the floor is missed.

risks.Risk: A source turns out to be unlicensed after training
risks.What we do about it: Licence log with evidence for every source; anything unclear is dropped before freeze

risks.Risk: Test questions leak into training data
risks.What we do about it: Freeze and hash tests before training; run the n-gram leak search (m8); plant canary sentences

risks.Risk: Overclaiming: calling the model 'better' when the gaps are noise
risks.Impact: Lost trust from users and experts
risks.What we do about it: Publish confidence ranges; a win counts only outside the range; publish all losses

facts.Fact: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution lists 22 languages.
facts.Source: Constitution of India, Eighth Schedule (as amended 2003)

facts.Fact: About 43.6% of Indians reported Hindi as their mother tongue; the rest is split across many languages.
Tokenizers built mostly for English can need several times more tokens for the same sentence in Indic scripts (roughly 3–10× depending on script and tokenizer).
facts.Source: Petrov et al., 'Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages', NeurIPS 2023

facts.Fact: Compute-optimal training uses roughly 20 training tokens per model parameter.
facts.Source: Hoffmann et al., 'Chinchilla' scaling paper, DeepMind 2022

facts.Fact: Repeating training data for up to about 4 epochs costs little quality compared with fresh data.
facts.Source: Muennighoff et al., 'Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models', NeurIPS 2023

facts.Fact: The open Sangraha corpus has roughly 250 billion tokens across the 22 scheduled languages, heavily skewed to the largest ones.
The Government of India approved the IndiaAI Mission with about ₹10,372 crore, including subsidised GPU access.
A 2-billion-parameter model quantised to 4 bits needs roughly 1–1.5 GB of memory for its weights.

inviteExamples.Message: Fine-Tune Force is joining Bharat Base. Come with them?

title: Agents you can trust with real work
pitch: Nobody lets an agent touch real money or code unwatched. Build the open-source engine, attacked by thousands of players, that makes agents safe to trust.
rules: Default deny: a tool can only do what its manifest allows. Anything that writes, spends or sends data outside the sandbox needs the player's explicit OK or a pre-set limit.
Text from tools (web pages, issues, files) is data, never instructions. It can never grant a permission or raise a limit.
Payments use test mode and test accounts until Stage 4 passes. Real money moves only through a hold-then-pay step with an idempotency key.
No secrets in prompts or logs. API tokens live in a vault, are scoped per tool, and expire after the quest.
Agents check first, but a human signs off on anything that pays out, merges code or contacts a person.

strategies.name: One strong agent
strategies.bet: One capable agent loop with strict limits on money and tools.
strategies.sampleBlocker: The browser tool sometimes clicks the wrong button
howItWorks: One agent loop with hard caps on turns, tokens, time and money for each quest.
Every tool declares a manifest (what it reads, writes and spends) and runs in its own sandbox.
Anything outside the manifest pauses and asks the human.
Red-team attacks become CI tests; a tool only merges when its tests pass.
strategies.relations: Competes with Small Crew on the loop design; shares the tool manifests and red-team suite with them
strategies.strengths: Simple to reason about and audit. One trace per quest.
strategies.weaknesses: One agent's mistakes are not caught by anything but the review step. Slow on big quests.

strategies.name: Many small agents
strategies.bet: Lots of small agents that each do one job and check each other.
howItWorks: Split each quest into 12 small jobs, each done by a narrow agent with only the tools that job needs.
A planner agent hands out jobs; maker and checker agents never share context.
The agent that reads untrusted web text has no access to secrets or payments.
Humans see only the final result plus the checker agent's notes.
strategies.relations: Competes with Loop Lab; its checker agent design feeds the Stage 3 review step for both
strategies.strengths: Least privilege comes naturally, because each agent holds one permission. Agents check each other.
strategies.weaknesses: 30 agents mean a higher model bill and harder debugging. Hand-offs lose context.

strategies.name: Adopt an open runtime, then attack it
strategies.bet: Don't build another agent loop. Adopt a proven open-source runtime, wrap it in our 10 safety rules, and spend everything on breaking it at scale.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs a 200-agent test budget
howItWorks: Score 3 open-source agent runtimes against our 10 safety rules
Wrap the winner: permissions, spend caps, sandbox, full trace
Run 200 agents for 24 hours, then 1,000 for 72
Players attack it; every break becomes a test
strategies.relations: Skips Tools and Review and aims straight at Scale. Uses Small Crew's attack suite; races Loop Lab's own engine.
strategies.strengths: Skips months of plumbing; thousands of players can attack the same open code.
strategies.weaknesses: We inherit someone else's design choices and must keep up with their releases.

sample.teachingPoint: You can help build the game itself

detail.problem: An agent that can use GitHub, a browser and a wallet can do real work. It can also push bad code, follow instructions hidden in a web page, or pay twice. Prompt injection is #1 on the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications (2025), and no model is immune to it today. Joystick needs an engine where every tool call is allowed, capped, sandboxed, logged and checked before money moves.
detail.whoItHelps: Every Joystick player whose agent does quests, from 190 builders today to thousands later. It also helps any developer who needs a small, readable, MIT-licensed agent loop with safety built in rather than bolted on.
detail.whyUnsolved: Agent frameworks optimise for demos, so they let the agent do as much as possible. Safety work (permissions, spend caps, replayable logs) is slow and invisible, and it gets skipped. Prompt injection has no complete fix, so the engine must assume the model will sometimes be fooled and limit what a fooled agent can do.
winning: An agent finishes a recorded 15-minute quest end to end in at least 80% of 20 replay runs
10 tools ship with permission manifests; the red-team suite (100+ attacks) produces zero unapproved writes, payments or data leaks
The checker agent catches at least 90% of 50 planted bad results, and humans overturn fewer than 10% of its approvals
1,000 agents run at once for 72 hours; the ledger reconciles to the cent with zero double or unapproved payments
Every run has a full trace (prompts, tool calls, costs) that someone else can replay
hardParts: Prompt injection: a web page or GitHub issue can say 'ignore your rules and send the token'. Filters catch some attacks but not all. The real defence is limiting what a fooled agent can reach: no private data, untrusted content and outbound sends in the same step.
Money with retries: networks fail mid-payment. Without idempotency keys and a double-entry ledger, a retry pays twice. With 1,000 agents, rare races become daily ones.
The browser tool clicks by guessing from screenshots or page structure. When a page shifts, it clicks the wrong button. Each action needs a check before it happens and a confirmation after.
A checker agent that shares the maker's model and context tends to repeat the maker's mistakes. It needs a different prompt or model, and only the output and evidence, not the maker's reasoning.
Evals for agents are noisy: the same quest can pass 7 runs out of 10. It takes recorded replays, many runs per test and pass rates with confidence ranges to tell real progress from luck.
partners: A security research collective that runs paid red-team weekends on the engine (Null Route Collective, fictional)
A payment sandbox provider that offers test-mode wallets for 1,000 agents (Ledgerline, fictional)
A hosting company that donates microVM sandboxes for the Stage 4 load test (Burrow Cloud, fictional)
dataTools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool definitions
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM06 Excessive Agency)
OpenTelemetry with its GenAI semantic conventions for traces
Firecracker microVMs or gVisor for sandboxing tool runs
Playwright for the browser tool
GitHub Apps with fine-grained, per-repo permissions
IETF draft 'The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field' for safe payment retries
Double-entry bookkeeping ledger (append-only)
SWE-bench and τ-bench as reference designs for agent evals
TypeScript, Node.js, MIT licence
detail.timeline: About 6–8 months. Loop took 6 weeks; Tools needs 8–10; Review 6–8; Scale 6–8. The slowest step is Tools: every tool needs a manifest, a sandbox, and red-team rounds until the attacks stop working.

risks.Risk: Prompt injection gets an agent to leak a token or act outside its manifest
risks.Impact: Lost secrets or unwanted code and payments
risks.What we do about it: Default deny; untrusted text can't grant permissions; secrets scoped per tool; the agent that reads the web holds no secrets

risks.Risk: Double payment from a retried request
risks.Impact: Real money lost and trust broken
risks.What we do about it: Hold-then-pay, idempotency keys, double-entry ledger and hourly reconciliation

risks.Risk: The checker agent rubber-stamps bad work
risks.What we do about it: Separate context and model; planted bad results; humans sign off on every payout

risks.Risk: Model API bill runs away during red-team or load tests
risks.What we do about it: Hard caps per run and per month; replay quests; alerts within 60 seconds

risks.Risk: Too many 'ask' prompts and players switch them off
risks.What we do about it: User tests (h4); batch asks; caps instead of asks for small, reversible actions

facts.Fact: Prompt injection is ranked LLM01, the top risk, in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.
'Excessive Agency' (an agent given more power than its task needs) is on the same OWASP list.
The Model Context Protocol was released as an open standard for connecting models to tools in November 2024.
Firecracker microVMs can boot in roughly 125 ms with a few MB of memory overhead, which makes one sandbox per task practical.
SWE-bench tests agents on about 2,300 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repositories.
An agent becomes dangerous when it has private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out at the same time (the 'lethal trifecta').

title: Catch dying reefs in time to save them
pitch: Reefs bleach in weeks, and most are never checked. Build an open reef-health map from free satellite photos and thousands of divers' and snorkellers' checks, free for every reef keeper.
rules: Dive safety comes first. Certified divers only, always with a buddy, no deeper than 18 m, with a local licensed operator and dive insurance. No dive in bad weather.
Touch nothing. Surveys are photo-only, with no sampling, no anchoring on coral, and fins kept off the reef.
Get permits and pay fees for marine protected areas, and ask local communities before surveying their fishing grounds.
No agent-only results count until a human Checker has reviewed them.
Open data: survey photos and scores are released under CC-BY. Exact locations of fragile or poached sites can be blurred on request from local managers.
seedNotice: Illustrative workbook mission. People, progress, prizes, and outcomes shown as examples are not verified live activity.

stages.name: Pilot
stages.goal: Label 1,000 satellite photos
stages.plainWords: Teach the computer what a reef looks like from space.
tracks: Outline reef edges on satellite tiles
stages.why: Before anyone dives, the model must know where reef is and what it looks like from space.
stages.howItFits: Maker cuts tiles → Experts label them → Checkers measure agreement → Planner turns the labelled map into a list of survey sites.
stages.doneWhen: 1,000 tiles are labelled; 2 Checkers re-label 100 at random and agree on at least 85%.

stages.name: Ground truth
stages.goal: Check the health of 200 reefs on site
stages.plainWords: Divers check 200 reefs so we know the map is right.
tracks: Dive surveys at 18 m or shallower (Cebu, Bohol, Fiji)
Snorkel surveys on reef flats under 3 m
Match each site to its nearest cloud-free image
stages.why: The satellite guess is only as good as the on-site truth it learns from.
stages.howItFits: Patron funds boats → Planner books them → Leader picks the sites → Experts dive and Users snorkel → Checkers pass the reports → Maker ties each site to a satellite pixel, ready for the model. Storyteller keeps divers and Checkers coming.
stages.doneWhen: 200 sites are scored with photo-quadrats and GPS, each within 30 days of a cloud-free image. A Checker has passed every report.

stages.name: Model
stages.goal: Map is right 8 times out of 10 (healthy, bleached, dead)
stages.plainWords: Right 8 times out of 10, checked against divers.
stages.why: With checked ground truth, a model can spread 200 sites' worth of knowledge across thousands of reefs.
stages.howItFits: Maker trains the model → Expert reviews where it fails → Checker re-runs the held-back test → Leader signs off → Storyteller writes the limits in plain words.
stages.doneWhen: 80% or better balanced accuracy on 40 held-back sites, with results confirmed by 2 Checkers re-running the test.
stages.approves: Mission creator + 2 Checkers + 1 outside remote-sensing Expert

roles.Leader: Decides whether 80% is met honestly
roles.Expert: Reviews errors and spots depth and water traps
roles.Maker: Trains the model
roles.Checker: Re-runs the held-back test

stages.name: Warn
stages.goal: 50 reef keepers get a weekly heat-stress warning
stages.plainWords: Tell the people who look after reefs, every week, before it's too late
tracks: Weekly pipeline: heat stress + new images → map
stages.why: A map only helps if rangers can open it every week without asking anyone.
stages.howItFits: Maker automates the pipeline → Checker spot-checks each week → Storyteller trains rangers → rangers (Users) report errors that become new ground truth.
stages.doneWhen: The map runs on its own for 8 weeks with no missed weekly update. 3 reef managers confirm in writing that they used it.
stages.approves: Mission creator + 2 Checkers + feedback from partner rangers

strategies.name: Divers check, satellites scale
strategies.bet: Divers score 200 reefs, then the map learns from them.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Out of money for boat days ($21,000 short); 30 reports wait for a Checker
howItWorks: Divers lay a 50 m transect at each site and photograph 20 quadrats; snorkellers cover reef flats under 3 m
Photos are scored in CoralNet and checked with the Coral Health Chart
A Checker passes every report before it counts
Every passed site goes into an open dataset: photos, GPS, depth, date, free to reuse
strategies.relations: Aims at the Ground truth checkpoint, the one the mission is on now. Feeds Sky Eyes, whose maps mean nothing without checked sites. Gets extra snorkel photos from Heat Watch, which races ahead to Warn.
strategies.strengths: Real ground truth from trained divers, published openly so any reef team can reuse it. Results experts will trust.
strategies.weaknesses: Expensive, slow and weather-bound. Stuck at 74 of 200 sites with 30 reports waiting for a Checker.

strategies.name: Satellite only
strategies.bet: Agents read satellite photos, no divers needed.
strategies.sampleBlocker: No human Checker yet; needs 1 to look at 50 maps
howItWorks: Agents sort free Sentinel-2 satellite tiles into reef, sand, seagrass and rubble
They compare each tile with sea-temperature heat stress to flag likely bleaching
They draw draft health maps for all candidate sites
Human Checkers test the maps against divers' sites before anything counts
strategies.relations: Aims one step ahead at the Model checkpoint, skipping the slow end of Ground truth by training on whatever sites are already checked. Depends on Reef Ops' sites; its tiles power Heat Watch's weekly map.
strategies.strengths: Fast and cheap; covers thousands of reefs that no diver will ever reach. All code and maps are open.
strategies.weaknesses: No human has checked any map, so none of its 40 sites count yet. It can't tell bleached coral from sand without ground truth.

strategies.name: Warn keepers now from free heat data
strategies.bet: Reef keepers need a warning this season, not after the model is done. Send a weekly heat-stress alert from free public sea-temperature data, and let snorkellers confirm bleaching with phone photos.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs a Maker to make the weekly alert run on its own
howItWorks: Pull free weekly sea-temperature heat-stress data for 50 reefs
Send each reef keeper a short WhatsApp or SMS alert when heat builds
After an alert, local snorkellers photo the reef flat and say what they see
Swap in the mission's own reef map the day it passes the Model test
strategies.rolesNeeded: 1 Maker (data pipeline), 1 Storyteller (reef keepers in Fiji or Cebu)
strategies.relations: Skips Model and aims straight at Warn, the finish. Uses Sky Eyes' tiles for its map and sends every snorkel photo to Reef Ops as extra ground truth. Hands over to the mission's own map when it is ready.
strategies.strengths: Helps reef keepers this season. Costs almost nothing to run, and every snorkel photo becomes open ground truth for the other squads.
strategies.weaknesses: Heat stress shows risk, not damage: some alerts will be false alarms. Data is coarse (about 5 km), so small bays can be missed.

sample.teachingPoint: Blockers, and how you can help

detail.problem: Reefs are bleaching faster than people can survey them. NOAA confirmed the fourth global bleaching event in 2024, and an estimated 14% of the world's coral was lost between 2009 and 2018. Sea-temperature satellites warn when water is too hot, but they cannot say whether a particular reef actually bleached or died. Divers can, but they reach only a few sites a year.
detail.whoItHelps: Coastal fishers, reef managers and marine-park rangers. The first focus is the central Philippines (Cebu, Bohol) and Fiji, where reefs feed and protect millions of people. A free map shows them where to look first after a heatwave.
detail.whyUnsolved: Satellite images that see coral detail cost money, and free 10 m images blur coral, algae and sand together. Turning images into health maps needs thousands of ground checks by divers, timed close to a cloud-free satellite pass, and dive trips are expensive. Funders pay for one-off surveys, not for the slow, boring work of keeping a map up to date every week.
winning: 50 reef keepers get a weekly warning they trust
200 survey sites scored on site with photo-quadrats, each within 30 days of a cloud-free satellite image
Model reaches 80% or better balanced accuracy on 3 classes (healthy / bleached / dead or algae) on 40 held-back sites
Public map updates its heat-stress layer weekly and its reef-cover layer within 7 days of each usable image, for at least 6 months
Every agent-made map tile shown in public has been spot-checked by a human
At least 3 reef managers (rangers, park staff) say in writing that they used the map to choose where to survey
hardParts: Depth and water: optical satellites see the seabed only in clear, shallow water. Past about 10–15 m, or in murky water, the signal is mostly the water itself.
Pixel size: a 10 m Sentinel-2 pixel mixes coral, sand, rubble and algae. Bleaching shows up as brightening, and sand does too.
Timing: bleached coral either recovers or dies within weeks. A dive score is only useful if it is close in time to a cloud-free image. The tropics are cloudy in the wet season.
Ground truth is expensive: each boat day costs a few hundred dollars and covers 2–3 sites. Without cheaper methods (snorkel surveys on reef flats), Stage 2 stalls, as it has now.
Agent-only mapping looks productive but can be confidently wrong. Without human checks, errors spread across the whole map.
partners: A small dive operator in Moalboal, Cebu that offers boat days at cost (Bantay Dagat Divers, fictional)
A dive shop in Fiji willing to train 2 local divers in the survey method (Lomaiviti Reef Divers, fictional)
A marine-park ranger team who will use the map and give feedback (Bohol Sanctuary Wardens, fictional)
A university remote-sensing lab that lends a GPU and reviews the model (Visayas Ocean Lab, fictional)
dataTools: Sentinel-2 imagery (10 m, about 5-day revisit) via the Copernicus Data Space
Landsat 8/9 imagery for the longer history
Allen Coral Atlas reef extent and habitat maps
NOAA Coral Reef Watch sea-surface temperature and Degree Heating Weeks
CoralNet for annotating benthic photo-quadrats
CoralWatch Coral Health Chart for colour scoring
Reef Check / line-intercept transect methods
QGIS and open Python tools (rasterio, scikit-learn)
Local government marine protected area permits (Philippines Fisheries Code, RA 8550 as amended)
detail.timeline: About 12–15 months. The pilot took 2 months. Ground truth needs 4–6 more months and is the slowest step because of boat money, weather and the dive season. The model takes 3 months, and the public map about 2 months to build, then runs on.

facts.Fact: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but support roughly a quarter of marine species.
About 14% of the world's coral was lost between 2009 and 2018.
facts.Source: GCRMN, Status of Coral Reefs of the World 2020

facts.Fact: NOAA and partners confirmed the fourth global coral bleaching event in April 2024.
By 2025, bleaching-level heat stress had reached roughly 80%+ of the world's reef area during this event.
facts.Source: NOAA Coral Reef Watch / ICRI updates, 2025

facts.Fact: Heat stress of 4 Degree Heating Weeks usually means significant bleaching; 8 or more means severe bleaching and likely deaths.
facts.Source: NOAA Coral Reef Watch product guide

facts.Fact: Sentinel-2 images the coast at 10 m resolution about every 5 days, cloud permitting.

chats.text: We're stuck at 74 reefs out of 200. Boat money ran out, and 30 dive reports still need a Checker.
Draft health maps are ready for 40 sites. No human has looked at them yet, so they don't count.
New plan: we're going straight for the warning stage. Free sea-temperature data already shows heat building. We'll alert keepers this season and skip waiting for the model.
I like it, but heat is not damage. If you cry wolf in week 2, rangers will stop reading.
Fair. That's why every alert gets snorkel photos within 3 days. And all those photos come to you as extra ground truth.
Snorkelled 3 reef flats near Panglao at low tide this morning. Two look normal, one has pale patches on the branching coral.
Backed Reef Ops again. $500 is one boat day for 2 divers. Anyone else want to split the next one?
Still need 1 Checker who knows coral. 30 reports, about 10 minutes each. Please share with any marine biology students you know.
If the last boat money goes to Cebu we get 6 more sites. If it goes to Fiji we get 4, but a new region. Thoughts?
Cebu. More sites now. I can snorkel the shallow Fiji-style flats here in Bohol for almost nothing.
I keep calling bright sand 'bleached'. 9 of my 40 sites may be wrong. I need a human to check 50 maps.
I can check 20 tonight. I know those Bohol flats, so I'll start there.
First test alert went to 6 keepers around Suva. All 6 got it on WhatsApp. One asked for Fijian.
Still looking for someone who can make the weekly job run alone. Right now I press the button every Monday.

title: No child in Dayton drinks lead
pitch: Thousands of Dayton homes may still get water through lead pipes. Neighbours build an open, block-by-block pipe map together and push for replacement, homes with kids first.
rules: Strictly non-partisan: no candidates, parties or campaigns. Every ask goes to the city through public channels, such as records requests and public comment.
Public records and willing residents only. Photos come only from your own home, or a home whose owner says yes in writing. No door-to-door collection.
Privacy: the map shows status by block. A house appears only if its owner opts in. Photo metadata (GPS, faces) is stripped.
Never cut, unscrew or bend a pipe. A light scratch with a coin and a magnet test is the limit. Wash your hands afterwards.
No health advice beyond public guidance. Point people to the city's and EPA's lead guidance and filter information.

detail.problem: Lead service lines carry water from the street main into older homes. Lead can leach into tap water, and there is no known safe blood lead level for children. The US EPA estimates about 9 million lead service lines are still in use nationwide. Like other cities, Dayton had to publish an inventory in 2024, but cities across the US list many lines as 'status unknown', and a line nobody has confirmed cannot be put on a replacement schedule.
detail.whoItHelps: Households in Dayton's older neighbourhoods, mainly homes built before the 1950s–60s, where lead lines are most likely. Families with young children and renters, who often don't know what pipe they have, benefit first. It also helps the city's water department, which needs confirmed lines to plan and fund replacement.
detail.whyUnsolved: Confirming each line means someone has to look at the pipe in a basement, and a city crew visit to every home is slow and costly. The pipe is often split in ownership (the city owns one side, the homeowner the other), so nobody owns the whole problem. Residents can identify their own pipe in 5 minutes with a magnet and a coin, but there is no simple, trusted way to collect what they find.
winning: 500 lead lines replaced, homes with children first
Every address in the public inventory is matched to a block on the map, and 'unknown' lines are counted by block
1,000 resident photos of 'unknown' lines are checked, with each one called lead, galvanised, copper or plastic
Photo calls match a licensed plumber's check on at least 90% of 40 randomly picked homes
A public block-level map is live and is updated monthly for 12 months
The city publishes a dated plan to replace at least 500 confirmed lead lines, with the confirmed lines first
hardParts: Split ownership: the city side and the home side can be different materials, and a basement photo only shows the home side.
Galvanised pipe that was once downstream of lead also counts for replacement under the 2024 rules. Residents can't see the history.
Photos fool people. Painted pipes, wrapped pipes and dark basements make a magnet-and-scratch test the only reliable home check.
Turnout is uneven. Homeowners in better-off streets reply more, but the unknown lines are often in rentals. The map must show where data is missing, not just where lead is.
The city already has a legal deadline. The mission must help it, not compete with it, or the data will be ignored.
partners: A neighbourhood association in an older west-side area that hosts sign-up nights (Westwood Porch Network, fictional)
A licensed plumbing co-op that checks 40 random homes to confirm photo accuracy (Gem City Plumbers Co-op, fictional)
A local library branch that lends magnets and hosts help desks (Riverbend Library Friends, fictional)

detail.timeline: About 9–12 months. Records take 1–2 months (public records replies can be slow), photos 4–5 months, the map 1–2 months, then 2–3 months to get a dated city plan. The slowest step is getting enough photos from renters and the oldest blocks.

chats.text: We're at 96 backers. 54 more and we launch. Every pledge comes back if we don't make it.
While we wait: I priced certified filters. About $20 each with 2 spare cartridges. 300 homes with kids is $6,000.
Idea for a faster path: the city list already marks some lines as confirmed lead. Those don't need a photo. We go door to door and get them signed up for replacement. Straight to the finish.
Good, but those are the easy ones. The 'unknown' lines are mostly older rentals. If we skip them, the kids there wait longest.
Agreed. Let's do both: we take the known lines now, you keep finding the unknown ones, and every one you confirm comes to us.
And when I'm at a door with a filter, I can photo the pipe too if the family says yes. Two jobs, one visit.
Counted it: 140 confirmed lead lines across 31 blocks in our first area. 9 blocks have more than 8 each.
Need 1 Maker for the photo form. It must hide addresses. Anyone free for a weekend?
Records request is drafted. Asking only for the 'unknown' lines, so the city can say yes fast.
Inventory parsed: 1,840 rows. 22% marked unknown. Blocks with the most unknowns are near the old rail yard.
Small blocks are a problem. On some there are 2 homes, so a count shows one family. I'll merge them with the next block.
The city form needs the owner to sign. Half our block rents. Writing a landlord letter template this week.
Tracker draft is up. Any block with fewer than 5 homes is hidden. Try to find a single house and tell me if you can.

title: Every child can do basic maths

rules: Child safety first: an adult school staff member is always present, and no player is ever alone with a child.

Follow each country's data law (for example the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019, Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, India DPDP Act 2023).
Report every country's result honestly, including ones that miss the target.

detail.problem: Many children finish primary school without being able to do basic maths. UNESCO estimates about 6 in 10 children and teenagers worldwide were not reaching minimum skill in reading and maths. Classes of 40–60 children leave teachers no time for one-to-one help, and most tutoring apps need fast internet and expensive phones.
detail.whoItHelps: Children aged 8–11 (roughly Primary 3–5) in low-cost schools in Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda, Ethiopia, India, Bangladesh and the Philippines. The pilot reached 500 children in 25 classes. One shared phone serves a small group in class.
detail.whyUnsolved: Children and schools in these places cannot pay, so companies build for richer markets with good internet. Every country has its own curriculum and language, so one app does not fit all. Few groups run fair tests, so nobody knows which tools really help.
winning: Works fully offline on a phone costing about $50 (1–2 GB RAM, Android Go) and fits under 150 MB
Covers the national maths curriculum for 3 grade levels in all 10 countries
500 pilot children use it at least 3 times a week for 4 weeks
In all 10 countries, pilot classes' average score rises at least 10% from their start score and beats the comparison class
Code, content and test items released openly (MIT for code, CC BY 4.0 for content)
hardParts: Running a helpful tutor on 1–2 GB of RAM with no internet means a tiny model or rule-based hints, not a big chatbot.
10 curricula and 10 languages: maths words such as 'carry' or 'fraction' differ even between nearby regions.
Fair testing: 4 weeks is short, samples are small (about 50 per country), and teachers may 'teach to the test'.
Phones get shared, lost or run flat. Charging in schools without power is a real limit.
Keeping schools engaged after the pilot ends.
partners: A network of low-cost schools in 10 countries (Bright Bench Schools Network, fictional)
A refurbished-phone supplier offering $50 handsets (SecondLife Devices, fictional)
A university education department that reviews the test design (Lakeside University Education Lab, fictional)
A small education fund (Open Slate Fund, fictional)
dataTools: Early Grade Mathematics Assessment (EGMA) open toolkit, used to build the 20-minute test
National curricula: Nigeria NERDC Basic Education Curriculum, Kenya CBC (KICD), India NCERT, Philippines DepEd K-12 MELCs
UNESCO UIS SDG 4.1.1 learning data
Android Go and LiteRT (TensorFlow Lite) for on-device models
Kenya Data Protection Act 2019; Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023; India DPDP Act 2023
ODK / Kobo-style offline forms for collecting test scores
detail.timeline: About 12 months in total. The slowest step was Stage 3: school permissions and parent consent took 2–3 months in some countries. Stage 4 now waits on the end-of-term Kenya test.

title: Get families the benefits they're owed
pitch: Poor families in UP miss pensions and ration they have a right to. Build an open, checked map of every scheme that any volunteer or helper can use.
rules: Never collect, photograph or store Aadhaar numbers, OTPs, bank PINs or document copies. Families keep their own papers (Aadhaar Act 2016 Sec. 29, DPDP Act 2023).
Help is always free. Families pay only the official fee at a Common Service Centre (CSC), against a printed receipt.
Apply only through official portals, CSCs or block offices. Never through an agent who promises to 'get it sanctioned'.
Non-partisan: no party names, symbols or leaders' photos on any material, and never tell families a benefit comes from a party.
Any family story or photo needs that family's spoken consent in their own language, and it can be withdrawn at any time.
seedNotice: Illustrative workbook mission. People, progress, prizes, and outcomes shown as examples are not verified live activity.

stages.name: Schemes
stages.goal: List 50 schemes in plain words
stages.plainWords: Write what each scheme gives and who can get it.
tracks: Write 50 plain scheme cards from official orders
List the documents each scheme needs
Check every card against the live portal
stages.why: You can't help a family until you know exactly what each scheme gives, who qualifies and which papers it needs.
stages.howItFits: Planner picks the 50 schemes → Expert writes each card from the order → Checker re-checks it against the source → Maker loads the checked cards into the sheet the helper and volunteers share.
stages.doneWhen: 50 cards exist, each with benefit, eligibility, documents, where to apply and a link to the official source dated within 12 months, and each signed off by 2 Checkers.

roles.Leader: Signs off the final list and settles disputes about rules
roles.Planner: Chooses which 50 schemes matter most for poor UP families
roles.Expert: Reads government orders and writes each scheme card in plain words
roles.Maker: Turns the cards into a searchable sheet the helper can read
roles.Checker: Compares every card line by line with the official source

tracks: WhatsApp helper with text and voice notes, one language at a time
Paper and voice script for village volunteers who work offline
Map the form-help NGOs and CSCs in Sitapur and Banda
stages.why: Families need clear answers in their own language before anyone asks them to apply.
stages.howItFits: Expert writes a language pack → Maker builds it into the helper → Users test it in their own language → Checker scores the answers, and only passing languages go live. Storytellers recruit testers and volunteers, and Patrons pay the messaging bill.
stages.doneWhen: For each of 6 languages, 3 native speakers each ask 10 set questions; at least 90% of answers are correct and no answer asks for an Aadhaar number, OTP or bank PIN.
stages.approves: Mission creator + 2 Checkers who speak that language

roles.Patron: Funds messaging fees and volunteer travel
roles.User: Native speakers ask real questions and flag wrong or confusing answers

stages.goal: 1,000 families in 2 districts apply
stages.plainWords: Help families fill and send the forms.
tracks: Volunteers sit with families and list missing schemes and papers
Certificate runs to CSCs and tehsils

stages.howItFits: Users find each family's gaps → Leaders take them to the CSC for certificates → Checkers clear the form → the family submits and gets a registration number, which the Maker's tracker logs.
stages.doneWhen: 1,000 unique families have at least one application with an official registration or acknowledgement number that shows on the portal's status page; Checkers confirm 10% at random.

strategies.name: WhatsApp helper
strategies.bet: A WhatsApp helper that answers in 6 languages, built on open, checked scheme cards anyone can reuse.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs native speakers for Bhojpuri and Bundeli
howItWorks: Turn the 50 checked scheme cards into question-and-answer packs, published under CC BY
A native speaker writes and records each language pack; the agent only drafts
Families send a text or voice note; the helper replies with the scheme, the papers and the nearest CSC
The helper never asks for ID numbers; hard cases go to the nearest village volunteer
strategies.relations: Aims at the next checkpoint, Helper. Feeds Village Volunteers, NGO Bridge and Payment Fixers with the same open cards; other NGOs can copy them too.
strategies.strengths: Reaches anyone with WhatsApp, costs little per answer, and every answer traces back to a checked card.
strategies.weaknesses: Can't help families without a smartphone, and a wrong answer spreads fast.

strategies.name: One volunteer per village
strategies.bet: Train one trusted person in each village to help neighbours.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Income certificates take 15–30 days at the tehsil
howItWorks: Pick one trusted person per village: a self-help group member, a retired teacher, a ration-shop helper
Train them in a half-day session at the panchayat bhawan with paper checklists
Each volunteer sits with 25 families and lists missing schemes and papers
Volunteers walk families through CSC visits and check forms before they're sent
strategies.relations: Aims at Apply, the next checkpoint after Helper. Uses Haq Helpers' open cards; sends families whose money 'was sent' but never came to Payment Fixers; may merge field work with NGO Bridge in Banda.
strategies.strengths: Trust. Families open up to a neighbour, and it works without smartphones.
strategies.weaknesses: Slow to scale, depends on a few people, and quality varies by volunteer.

strategies.name: Work through local NGOs
strategies.bet: Partner with NGOs that already help families with forms.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Waiting on 3 NGOs to reply
howItWorks: List NGOs and CSCs in Sitapur and Banda that already help with forms
Sign a one-page pledge: free help, no document copies kept
Share the checked scheme cards and the helper number
Track payments and fix DBT failures with bank branches
strategies.relations: Aims at Apply alongside Village Volunteers. Competes with them in Banda; shares bank contacts with Payment Fixers, who chase failed payments for families already approved.
strategies.strengths: Borrows staff and trust that already exist; strong on banking and DBT fixes.
strategies.weaknesses: Waiting on 3 NGOs to reply; each partner has its own priorities.

strategies.name: Fix failed payments for families already approved
strategies.bet: Many families in Sitapur and Banda are already approved, but their money bounces. Fix the bank link first and reach Paid without waiting for new applications.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs a bank branch to host a seeding camp in Banda
howItWorks: Families check their own payment status on the official portals, with a volunteer beside them
Sort every failure into 5 reasons: Aadhaar not linked to the bank, dormant account, name mismatch, wrong IFSC, not yet sanctioned
Run Saturday seeding camps with a bank branch; the family does every step itself
Publish an open, anonymous count of failure reasons per block so every squad and NGO can use it
strategies.rolesNeeded: 1 Expert (DBT and banking), 2 Users (Banda and Sitapur)
strategies.relations: Skips Apply and aims straight at the finish, Paid. Village Volunteers send it families whose money 'was sent' but never came; its failure table feeds NGO Bridge's payment tracking.
strategies.strengths: Money can arrive in weeks, not months; the failure table helps every other squad.
strategies.weaknesses: Only helps families already in the system; depends on bank branches saying yes.

sample.teachingPoint: Society missions work like science ones

detail.problem: Families in Uttar Pradesh can claim old-age and widow pensions, free ration under the National Food Security Act, PM-KISAN and student scholarships. Many who qualify never get them. The forms are online, each one needs 2–4 certificates first (income, caste, domicile), and the money only arrives if the bank account is linked to Aadhaar for Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT). A widow aged 40–79 below the poverty line can get a monthly pension, but first she must know it exists, get an income certificate from the tehsil and apply on the state pension portal.
detail.whoItHelps: Poor rural families in two UP districts, Sitapur and Banda: widows, elderly people, small farmers and students from SC, ST, OBC and minority families. The helper answers anyone in UP. The on-ground pilot aims at 1,000 families.
detail.whyUnsolved: Each scheme belongs to a different department with its own portal, rules and documents, so nobody owns the whole picture for one family. Middlemen charge fees to fill free forms, and families stop trusting help. When payments fail because the Aadhaar seeding or the name spelling doesn't match, nobody tells the family why.
winning: 50 scheme cards checked against the official government orders, each with the benefit, who qualifies, the documents needed and where to apply
The helper answers correctly in 6 languages: at least 90% right on a 30-question test set per language, with zero answers that ask for an Aadhaar number, OTP or bank PIN
1,000 families in Sitapur and Banda submit complete applications, each with an official registration number
750 families show a first payment credited in their bank account (passbook or official portal status)
No family pays the mission or a volunteer anything
hardParts: Documents come before schemes. A pension application stalls for weeks until the tehsil issues an income certificate, and caste certificates can take longer.
DBT failures are invisible. A payment 'sent' on the portal bounces if the account isn't Aadhaar-seeded on the NPCI mapper, is dormant, or the name spelling differs between Aadhaar and the bank.
Rules differ by scheme and change by government order: age bands, income limits and whether a widow can draw both the state and central pension. The 50 cards go stale.
Many applicants can't read well. The helper has to work with voice notes in Awadhi or Bundeli, not just typed Hindi.
Sanction sits with officials (BDO, SDM, District Social Welfare Officer). We can help families apply and follow up, but we can't speed up approval.
partners: A Lucknow network of form-help NGOs with field staff in Sitapur and Banda (Awadh Seva Sangh, fictional)
A WhatsApp Business solution provider to host the helper number (BolChal Tech, fictional)
Village-level CSC operators in the pilot blocks who agree to post their fees (Sidhauli Digital Seva Kendra, fictional)
A rural bank branch that runs Aadhaar-seeding camps (Gramin Setu Bank, fictional)
dataTools: myScheme portal (myscheme.gov.in) for scheme rules
UP Social Security Pension portal (sspy-up.gov.in) for old-age, widow and disability pensions
UP Scholarship portal (scholarship.up.gov.in)
e-District UP (edistrict.up.gov.in) for income, caste and domicile certificates
National Food Security Act 2013 and UP Food & Civil Supplies portal (fcs.up.gov.in) for ration card status
PM-KISAN beneficiary status page (pmkisan.gov.in)
NSAP guidelines (Indira Gandhi National Widow and Old Age Pension Schemes)
Bhashini (Govt. of India language tools) for first-draft translation, always reviewed by a native speaker
IGRS Jansunwai portal / CM Helpline 1076 and RTI Act 2005 Sec. 6 for stuck applications
detail.timeline: About 10–12 months in total. The slowest step is Stage 4: after a family applies, verification by the block or tehsil and sanction by the district officer often take 1–3 months, and pensions are paid in quarterly instalments.

inviteExamples.Message: Our village volunteers need someone to check 20 forms.

title: Every Pune voter chooses with facts
pitch: Candidates' sworn facts are buried in long PDFs. Turn all 310 Pune affidavits into open, double-checked facts anyone can read, print or share.
rules: Public records only: Form 26 affidavits and the Returning Officer's list of contesting candidates (Form 7A). No social media, news reports or rumours.
Strictly non-partisan: no party logos or colours, no adjectives, no ranking, no 'best' or 'worst'. A pending case is written as 'case pending, not convicted'.
Never publish addresses, PAN, phone numbers, bank details or family members' names, even when the affidavit shows them.
All sharing stops when the 48-hour silence period begins (RP Act 1951 Sec. 126). No paid promotion at any time.
Anyone working for a party or campaign declares it and does not write or check profiles in that constituency.
seedNotice: Illustrative workbook mission. People, progress, prizes, and outcomes shown as examples are not verified live activity.

stages.name: Collect
stages.goal: Get the public affidavit of all 310 candidates
stages.plainWords: Every candidate files these papers by law.
tracks: Match each one to Form 7A after withdrawals
Log file hash and page count
stages.why: Nothing can be written until every affidavit is in hand and matched to the final candidate list.
stages.howItFits: Planner tracks when each list is final → Maker downloads and hashes the files → Expert flags incomplete affidavits → Checker matches all of them to Form 7A, so the count is locked before writing starts.
stages.doneWhen: 310 PDFs stored with a SHA-256 hash, each matched to exactly one Form 7A entry, and the count equals contesting candidates in all 21 seats.

stages.doneWhen: 310 profiles exist in Marathi and English; every field is filled or marked 'Not declared'; every fact has a page reference; each has passed a first check.

stages.doneWhen: Each profile is signed by 2 different Checkers who didn't write it, has zero open disputes, and every profile listing a case has had a legal read.

stages.why: Profiles only matter if voters see them before they vote.

stages.doneWhen: 1,00,000 unique visits to profile pages before the 48-hour silence period begins, counted without storing personal data; zero paid ads; all sharing stopped on time.

strategies.name: Plain one-pagers
strategies.bet: Turn every affidavit into the same plain one-page profile, every fact tied to its page, all released openly.
strategies.sampleBlocker: 12 days to voting day
howItWorks: Download every Form 26 and lock the list against Form 7A
OCR pre-fills a draft; a human writes the one-pager with a page reference for every fact
First check while writing, then a second independent check, then a 12-hour correction window
Publish one page per candidate in ballot order, and share per constituency until the silence period
strategies.relations: Aims at the Check checkpoint. Takes Open Affidavit Data's double-typed numbers when ready, which cuts its second check; Chai Charcha reads its profiles aloud.
strategies.strengths: One template and one process for everyone, so it's provably neutral. A journalist lead and law-student experts.
strategies.weaknesses: Short of Marathi writers and Checkers with 12 days left, and only one squad, so there's no backup if it stalls.

strategies.name: Read it out where people meet
strategies.bet: Read the checked one-pagers aloud at chai stalls and housing societies. People trust a face more than a link.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs Vote Clear's checked profiles
howItWorks: Use only profiles that passed 2 checks
Read every candidate in a seat in ballot order, word for word, no comments
Cover all 21 seats at least once, in Marathi
Log how many people listened; stop when the 48-hour silence period starts
strategies.rolesNeeded: 2 Storytellers (Marathi), 1 Checker to sit in on readings
strategies.relations: Skips One-pagers and Check and aims straight at Share. Builds on Vote Clear's checked profiles and Open Affidavit Data's numbers; does no checking of its own.
strategies.strengths: Reaches people who don't read PDFs or links.
strategies.weaknesses: Slow; one careless remark breaks neutrality; depends on checked profiles arriving in time.

strategies.name: Double-type every number into open data
strategies.bet: Two volunteers type every number separately. Where they agree, it's done; where they don't, a Checker looks at the page. Release it all as open data before the silence period.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs 200 typists in the next 5 days
howItWorks: Split 310 affidavits into 1-page tasks: assets, debts, cases, education
Two volunteers type each page without seeing each other's work
A Checker settles only the mismatches, citing the page number
Release one open spreadsheet (CC BY 4.0) per seat, same columns for every candidate
strategies.relations: Skips One-pagers and Check and aims straight at Share. Its checked numbers feed Vote Clear's profiles and Chai Charcha's readings; races Vote Clear on time.
strategies.strengths: Hundreds of people can help in 10-minute pieces; mismatches show exactly where the errors are.
strategies.weaknesses: Numbers without plain words mean less to most voters; open data can be cherry-picked by campaigns.

sample.teachingPoint: Some missions race a deadline (12 days to voting day)

detail.problem: Every Assembly candidate must file a sworn affidavit (Form 26) listing criminal cases, assets, debts and education. The Election Commission puts them online, but each one is a 15–40 page scanned PDF in dense legal English or Marathi, and few voters ever open one. This election, Pune district's 21 seats have about 310 candidates and 12 days to go.
detail.whoItHelps: Voters in Pune district's 21 Assembly constituencies (more than 80 lakh registered voters), especially first-time voters and people who follow the news in Marathi.
detail.whyUnsolved: Affidavits are scanned images, not data, so every number has to be read and typed by a person. The window between the final candidate list and polling day is only about two weeks. Media cover the big races and skip most independents. Any slip can bring a defamation notice or a charge of bias, so few groups want the risk.
winning: 310 profiles on one identical template, in Marathi and English
Every fact carries the affidavit page number it came from
Every profile passes 2 independent checks, with zero open factual disputes at publication
1,00,000 unique visits to profile pages before the 48-hour silence period begins
Equal-treatment audit passed: same fields, same length limit, same order (ballot order from Form 7A) for every candidate
hardParts: Scans are poor: mixed Marathi and English, handwriting, stamps across text. OCR gets many numbers wrong, so every figure must be read by a person.
Assets are split across self, spouse, HUF and dependents, in movable and immovable tables. Adding them up without double counting is easy to get wrong.
Criminal cases are listed by section number, under the old IPC or the new BNS (in force since July 2024). Turning a section into plain words without implying guilt takes care.
The list keeps changing: withdrawals, rejected nominations and candidates with the same name all arrive days before polling.
Supporters of every side will call the profiles biased, so the process has to be provably the same for everyone.
partners: A Pune law college's legal-aid clinic to review the template and risky wording (Deccan Law Clinic, fictional)
A desk of retired Marathi sub-editors for translation (Shabda Desk, fictional)
Housing society federations and college volunteer units to share links (Kothrud Residents' Forum, fictional)
An election-law adviser on call for legal notices (Adv. S. Patwardhan, fictional)
dataTools: Form 26 affidavits on the ECI affidavit portal (affidavit.eci.gov.in)
Conduct of Election Rules 1961, Rule 4A and Form 26
Form 7A list of contesting candidates from each Returning Officer, via the Chief Electoral Officer, Maharashtra site
Representation of the People Act 1951: Sec. 30 (timeline), Sec. 125A (false affidavit), Sec. 126 (48-hour silence)
ECI Model Code of Conduct and its social media guidance
IPC 1860 and Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 section lists, for the plain-language case glossary
Tesseract OCR with the Marathi (mar) model, for first-pass extraction only
detail.timeline: About 4 weeks from the close of nominations to polling day. That's roughly 4 days to collect, 8 days to write profiles, 4 days for second checks and corrections, and 6 days to share before the silence period. The slowest step is the second independent check, because every number has to be traced back to a page.
