inviteExamples.Message: 12 days to voting day. Can you check 10 profiles tonight?

title: No rider hurt by a Bengaluru pothole
pitch: Potholes throw Bengaluru's riders off their bikes every week. Build an open map with thousands of riders, and get the worst ones fixed for good.
rules: Never photograph from a moving vehicle or while standing in traffic. Pull over first or skip it.
No faces or number plates in photos. Blur them before uploading.
One pin per pothole. File only through official channels, from your own account. No fake, duplicate or bulk bot complaints.
Publish ward and office numbers, never personal attacks on named engineers or workers.
Non-partisan: no party or candidate branding, and the data is shared equally with anyone who asks.
seedNotice: Illustrative workbook mission. People, progress, prizes, and outcomes shown as examples are not verified live activity.

stages.name: Map
stages.goal: Pin 5,000 potholes
stages.plainWords: Photo and pin every pothole you pass.
tracks: Riders and commuters pin on daily routes
stages.why: You can't file or chase what nobody has located and proved with a photo.
stages.howItFits: Planner picks wards → Leader brings riders in → Users pin → Checker removes repeats → Expert tags the road owner → Maker's scoreboard shows each ward's count. Storyteller recruits more riders and Patron pays for the pins.
stages.doneWhen: 5,000 unique pins, each with photo, GPS, timestamp, size class and road owner; duplicates removed; a 5% random re-visit confirms at least 95% are real.

roles.Leader: Brings rider groups and RWAs on board
roles.Planner: Picks wards and fills gaps in coverage
roles.Expert: Tags who owns each road
roles.Maker: Runs the pin form and builds the ward scoreboard
roles.Checker: Removes duplicates and re-visits a random 5%
roles.Storyteller: Makes the 30-second 'how to pin safely' video
roles.User: Photos and pins potholes on routes they already take

stages.name: File
stages.goal: File every pothole with the city
stages.plainWords: Agents file the complaints for you.
tracks: Humans file from their own accounts
Route non-city roads to the right owner
stages.why: A pothole only enters the city's system once it has an official complaint ID.
stages.howItFits: Expert decides the owner → Maker drafts the complaint → Planner hands batches to many Users → Users file them → Checker confirms each ID is real.
stages.doneWhen: Every verified pin has an official complaint ID, or a logged reason why not (for example a private road); 10% of IDs are looked up and confirmed.

roles.Planner: Spreads filing across people so no account is flagged
roles.Expert: Routes metro, NHAI and utility-trench pins to the right office
roles.Maker: Drafts complaint text with location, landmark and photo
roles.Checker: Looks up complaint IDs to confirm they exist
roles.User: Files drafts from their own Sahaaya login

stages.name: Track
stages.goal: Chase every complaint until it's fixed
stages.plainWords: Follow up so none are forgotten.
stages.why: Complaints get forgotten without steady, polite follow-up.
stages.howItFits: Maker's scoreboard flags stale complaints → Planner queues them → Leader escalates → Storyteller puts ward numbers in front of officials in public meetings.
stages.doneWhen: Every open complaint has a logged follow-up at day 15, 30 and 60, and every complaint older than 30 days has been escalated with a reply recorded or an RTI filed.

roles.Leader: Chases old complaints with the ward engineer
roles.Planner: Queues follow-ups and RTIs
roles.Maker: Keeps the scoreboard updating weekly
roles.Storyteller: Presents the scoreboard at ward committee meetings
roles.User: Reports a pothole that reopens on their route

stages.name: Fixed
stages.goal: 80% fixed within 90 days
stages.plainWords: Most of them actually get fixed.
stages.why: The only result that matters is a road you can ride over safely.
stages.howItFits: Checker photographs each closure → Expert judges the repair → Planner counts the fix rate per ward → Storyteller shares the report.
stages.doneWhen: At least 80% of filed potholes have an after-photo, taken within 90 days of filing by someone other than the original pinner, showing a level repair; sunken or crumbling patches count as not fixed.

roles.Planner: Writes the 90-day ward report
roles.Expert: Judges whether a patch is level and lasting
roles.Checker: Visits 'closed' complaints and takes after-photos
roles.Storyteller: Shares the results with RWAs and the media

stages.name: Safer
stages.goal: Pothole crashes on mapped roads fall by half
stages.plainWords: Fewer riders get hurt
stages.why: Fixed potholes only matter if fewer people fall.
stages.doneWhen: Crash reports on mapped roads down 50% against the same months last year

strategies.name: Riders pin as they ride
strategies.bet: Delivery riders and commuters pin potholes on routes they already take, onto one open map anyone can download.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Residential lanes in 4 wards have almost no pins
howItWorks: Riders and commuters pin potholes on routes they already travel, but only when stopped
Checkers merge duplicates within 15 m and tag the road owner
Agents draft complaints; people file them from their own accounts
Follow up at day 15, 30 and 60, then return for an after-photo
strategies.rolesNeeded: Anyone with a phone; 2 Checkers; 1 Expert (road ownership)
strategies.relations: Aims at File, the next checkpoint. Crash Map ranks its pins by crashes; Fix It Right uses its pins and sends back a repair checklist for its Checkers.
strategies.strengths: Huge free coverage from people already on the road. Simple quests.
strategies.weaknesses: Pins cluster on delivery routes and miss residential lanes. One big squad, so quality varies.

strategies.name: Worst first
strategies.bet: Start where riders actually crash, not where potholes are. Push the 100 worst spots to the front of the queue.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs crash records by road
howItWorks: Gather public crash reports that name a road
Match each to pinned potholes within 50 metres
Rank road stretches by crashes and publish the open ranking
Chase the top 100 complaints every 15 days until fixed
strategies.relations: Skips File and aims at Track: it chases its top 100 spots while Pothole Patrol files the rest. Feeds its ranking to Fix It Right.
strategies.strengths: Fixes what hurts people first; the ranking is open for anyone to check.

strategies.bet: Patching pothole by pothole never ends. Take the 10 stretches where riders crash most, get them properly relaid through ward committees, and show crashes fall.

sample.teachingPoint: Lots of quick quests on your way home

detail.problem: Bengaluru has roughly 13,000–14,000 km of city-run roads, and potholes come back after every monsoon. People complain on the city's Sahaaya app or the 1533 helpline, but many complaints are closed without a repair, and nobody publishes ward-by-ward fix rates. Two-wheeler riders take most of the risk.
detail.whoItHelps: Bengaluru's 1.3 crore or so residents, above all two-wheeler riders, delivery workers, cyclists and pedestrians. The pilot covers 20 wards in the east and south of the city, then expands.
detail.whyUnsolved: Roads belong to different owners: the city corporation, BDA, NHAI, metro works, and water or power utilities that dig trenches. Each can point at another. Contractors are paid per job, and defect-liability clauses that should force free re-repair are rarely enforced. The complaint system measures closure, not repair, and city governance and ward maps are being reorganised, so it's often unclear which officer is responsible.
winning: Pothole crashes on mapped roads fall by half
5,000 unique potholes pinned, each with a photo, GPS, time, size and road owner
At least 95% of verified pins filed through an official channel, each with a complaint ID
80% of filed potholes show a verified repair (after-photo) within 90 days
A public ward scoreboard showing median days to fix, updated weekly
Zero road-safety incidents among players
hardParts: Duplicates: phone GPS drifts 5–20 m between buildings, so two riders pin the same pothole as two.
Road ownership: a pothole inside a metro work zone or over a water-board trench is not the corporation's job, and the complaint bounces.
'Closed' is not 'fixed'. Proving a repair needs a second visit and an after-photo.
Monsoon patches with cold mix often fail within weeks, so a 'fixed' pothole can reopen before day 90.
Ward boundaries and officer lists are changing under the new city corporations, so pins must be re-mapped when new boundaries are published.
partners: Delivery-rider community groups who pin on routes they already ride (Rider Saathi Collective, fictional)
Resident welfare associations in pilot wards (South-East RWA Forum, fictional)
A civic-tech volunteer group to host the map and scoreboard (OpenRaasta Labs, fictional)
A retired road engineer to judge repair quality (Kere Roads Advisory, fictional)
dataTools: Sahaaya grievance app and the 1533 helpline (the city's official complaint channels)
Greater Bengaluru Governance Act 2024 (city corporations and ward committees)
BBMP 198-ward boundary files on open civic data portals, plus newly notified ward maps when published
OpenStreetMap road network for snapping pins to roads
IRC:82 Code of Practice for Maintenance of Bituminous Roads (Indian Roads Congress)
RTI Act 2005 Sec. 6 for road work orders and defect-liability periods
Karnataka Public Procurement portal (KPPP) for road repair tenders
detail.timeline: About 7–9 months. That's 6–8 weeks to map, 3–4 weeks to file, then a 90-day tracking window for the last batch. The slowest step is waiting for repairs: crews prioritise main roads and hold back work in heavy rain.

budget.Note: About 3,500 paid pins; many are pinned free
For work orders and defect-liability periods
The largest cost; it proves the result

risks.Risk: A player is hurt while pinning
risks.What we do about it: Stop-first rule, safety video, no pins on fast roads, daylight re-visits
Each person files 10 at most per day from their own account; batches spread across people
After-photo rule; engineer review; RTI on repeat closures
Re-check at 30 days; re-file reopened potholes; push for hot-mix repairs in dry weeks
Store raw GPS; re-join pins to new boundaries when notified

facts.Fact: Sahaaya and the 1533 helpline are the city's official channels for civic complaints, potholes included.
BBMP had 198 wards from 2010. Its elected council's term ended in September 2020, and the city was run by administrators after that.
The Greater Bengaluru Governance Act 2024 replaced BBMP with the Greater Bengaluru Authority, which oversees several new city corporations notified in 2025.
Bengaluru has roughly 13,000–14,000 km of roads under the city corporation(s).
facts.Source: BBMP road infrastructure figures, various years

facts.Fact: A smartphone's GPS is typically accurate to about 5 m in open sky, and worse near tall buildings.
Bengaluru crossed 1 crore registered vehicles in 2023, most of them two-wheelers.

chats.text: 1,240 pins so far. The open map shows every pin with photo, size and road owner, and anyone can download it.
Pinned 40 this week on Outer Ring Road. Always pulled over first, promise.
We matched 200 crash reports to pins. 38 of them are on just 6 stretches.
That's why we're aiming straight at the finish: fewer crashes. Take the 10 worst stretches and get them relaid, not patched.
Love the aim, but skipping filing worries me. Without complaint numbers the ward scoreboard stays empty.
We'll still file through your process. We just won't wait for 5,000 pins before going to ward committees.
Counted near-misses at one Bellandur junction for an hour: 9 riders swerved hard. Stood on the footpath the whole time.
The patch on Sarjapur Road from last month is open again. 'Fixed' for 3 weeks, broken again in 3 more.
Coverage gap: residential lanes in 4 wards have almost no pins. Who lives near HSR Layout?
I can do HSR lanes after my last delivery, around 9 pm. Only when parked.
Crash data is patchy. Some reports just say 'near the flyover'. We're dropping those for now.
Repair checklist draft: 10 points from the road code. Square cut, clean, tack coat, pressed down, level with the road.
Ward committee meets on the 2nd Saturday. Can someone print before photos?
I'll print them. Keep faces and number plates out.

title: Every rupee reaches Bihar's schools
pitch: School money in Bihar is sent but often never arrives. Build an open ledger of 100 schools from public data, replies and visits, and get the gaps fixed.
rules: Strictly non-partisan. No party names, no politicians, no blame language. Report what the papers say and what we saw.
Public records only. No children's faces or names in photos. No staff personal data beyond name and post as given in the RTI reply.
On-ground visits only in school hours, in pairs, after the head teacher says yes. No entry if refused. Note the refusal and leave.
Each school gets 15 days to answer before its report card is published, and the answer is printed beside our findings.
No bribes and no 'speed money', ever. If someone asks for one, log it and leave.
seedNotice: Illustrative workbook mission. People, progress, prizes, and outcomes shown as examples are not verified live activity.

strategies.name: File and follow up in person
strategies.bet: File every request, and appeal in person when replies are late.
strategies.sampleBlocker: 59 late replies need appeals filed in person
howItWorks: Retired teachers in each district own 25 schools each.
One standard request goes to every block PIO, filed by registered post with a ₹10 postal order.
A shared tracker flags day 30 (reply due), day 60 (file first appeal) and day 90+ (second appeal).
Late appeals are grouped by district office so one trip files 5 to 10 appeals and comes back with stamped receipts.
Students code replies into a sheet. Two Checkers re-read 1 in 5.
strategies.rolesNeeded: 4 Experts in Bihar for appeals (1 each in Gaya, Muzaffarpur, Purnia, Patna), 2 Checkers to code replies
strategies.relations: Aims at Replies, the current checkpoint. Its open tracker, appeal templates and coded replies feed Open Ledger and Parent Panel.
strategies.strengths: Retired teachers know how block offices work, speak Hindi and Bhojpuri, and are taken seriously by officials.
strategies.weaknesses: Only 5 people, mostly in Patna. Appeals in Gaya and Purnia wait for someone to travel, and Commission hearings need a person in Patna.

strategies.name: Parents ask at the school
strategies.bet: Parents on School Management Committees ask about the school's own accounts at their meetings, and keep asking until the missing thing arrives.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Needs committee members willing to try
howItWorks: Make an open one-page Hindi guide to the school grant
Train 10 committee parents in Gaya and Patna
They ask 5 polite questions at the next meeting and note the answers
Follow each missing item, like a toilet door or library books, until it is there

sample.teachingPoint: Real-world blockers need people, not just agents

detail.problem: Every year each Bihar government school gets grants under Samagra Shiksha, for example a composite school grant of ₹10,000 to ₹1,00,000 depending on how many children are enrolled. Parents almost never see how much came in or what it bought. Toilets show up as 'functional' on UDISE+ but are locked or broken, and library books are bought on paper but not on the shelf.
detail.whoItHelps: Parents, School Management Committee (Vidyalaya Shiksha Samiti) members and teachers at 100 government primary and middle schools in Patna, Gaya, Muzaffarpur and Purnia districts. Roughly 25,000 to 35,000 children study there.
detail.whyUnsolved: The money flows through block and district offices, so no one at the school level sees the whole picture. RTI replies often come late, appeals take many months, and one parent asking alone is easy to ignore. Comparing paper with reality takes 100 site visits, and nobody is paid to do them.
winning: 50 schools get what was missing
100 RTI replies received (or a Commission order for each missing one)
100 school visits done with a 12-item checklist and timestamped photos
100 one-page report cards published in Hindi, each with the school's right of reply attached
Every gap above ₹5,000 or one missing facility backed by two documents (RTI reply + visit photo)
Report cards presented at 20 or more School Management Committee meetings
hardParts: PIOs transfer applications under Sec. 6(3) or reply 'information not held', and every transfer restarts a 5-day clock and a new paper trail.
Replies arrive as scanned cashbooks and PFMS printouts in mixed Hindi and English. Turning them into comparable numbers is slow, careful work.
Second appeals at the State Information Commission can wait months for a hearing, and the hearing is in Patna, far from rural applicants.
Grant heads differ by year and by school category, so 'missing money' is often a coding difference rather than theft. You have to know the Samagra Shiksha norms to tell which.
Head teachers may feel accused. Without their trust, visits get refused.
partners: A retired-teachers' association that lends volunteers for appeals and visits (Purana Shikshak Manch, fictional)
A law-college RTI clinic that checks appeal drafts (Patliputra Law Clinic, fictional)
A parents' network active in 20 School Management Committees (Abhibhavak Sangh Bihar, fictional)
dataTools: RTI Act 2005: Sec. 6 (application), Sec. 7(1) (30-day reply), Sec. 7(5) (no fee for BPL), Sec. 19(1) and 19(3) (first and second appeal), Sec. 20 (penalty)
Bihar Right to Information Rules 2006 (₹10 fee by cash, demand draft or postal order)
UDISE+ school-level data (enrolment, toilets, library, teachers) and school report cards
Samagra Shiksha Framework for Implementation (composite school grant norms) and Bihar PAB minutes
PFMS fund-transfer records as supplied in RTI replies
India Post registered post tracking (proof of filing)
detail.timeline: About 12 to 15 months in total. The slowest step is stage 3: 30 days for a reply, 30 to 45 days for a first appeal, then often 4 to 9 months before a second appeal is heard at the Commission.

budget.Item: School selection and UDISE+ data cleaning
Travel to district offices for 59 first appeals
Second appeals and Patna hearing travel

risks.Risk: Appeal deadlines lapse because nobody is free to travel
risks.Impact: Right to appeal lost for that request; must re-file and restart
risks.What we do about it: Tracker alerts at day 50; post appeals by registered post as a fallback

risks.Risk: Commission hearing scheduled at short notice in Patna
risks.Impact: Case adjourned or dismissed for non-appearance
risks.What we do about it: Patna-based volunteer holds written authority to attend

risks.Risk: Head teachers feel accused and refuse visits
risks.What we do about it: Retired teachers make first contact; share findings privately first

risks.Risk: Misreading a coding difference as missing money
risks.Impact: Unfair report card and loss of trust
risks.What we do about it: Two-document rule and right of reply

risks.Risk: Volunteer pressured or threatened at an office
risks.What we do about it: Pairs only, office hours only, leave and report, never argue

facts.Fact: A PIO must reply within 30 days of receiving an RTI application.
A first appeal can be filed within 30 days after the reply deadline passes, and must be decided within 30 days (45 at most).
A second appeal to the State Information Commission can be filed within 90 days of the first-appeal decision or deadline.
The application fee in Bihar is ₹10. People below the poverty line pay nothing.
facts.Source: Bihar RTI Rules 2006; RTI Act 2005 Sec. 7(5)

facts.Fact: The Commission can fine a PIO ₹250 a day for a late reply, up to ₹25,000.
The composite school grant ranges from ₹10,000 to ₹1,00,000 a year by enrolment band, and at least 10% is meant for sanitation (Swachhta Action Plan).
facts.Source: Samagra Shiksha Framework for Implementation (Ministry of Education, 2018 onward)

facts.Fact: Bihar has roughly 70,000 to 80,000 government schools.

title: No Lagos family caught by a flood
pitch: Floods hit Lagos streets with no warning. Build an open flood map and cheap open-hardware river gauges, kept alive by neighbours, so families get two hours to move.
rules: Never install or check sensors when water is rising or after dark. Two people at every river visit.
Opt-in only. Phone numbers are stored encrypted, used only for flood alerts, and deleted on 'STOP'.
Alerts say what the water is doing and what to do. They never blame anyone and never contradict official LASEMA or NEMA evacuation orders.
Every sensor site needs written OK from the landowner or community, plus the CDA chair.
Open hardware and open data. Water-level readings are published so others can reuse them.
seedNotice: Illustrative workbook mission. People, progress, prizes, and outcomes shown as examples are not verified live activity.

stages.name: Sensors
stages.goal: Put 14 water gauges and 6 rain gauges in place
stages.plainWords: First plan is waiting for the creator's OK.
stages.why: Without trusted readings, any alert is a guess.
stages.howItFits: Users and Storyteller show where water comes first → Planner turns that into candidate sites → Expert finds who must approve → Leader gets the OKs → Maker installs → Checker confirms 14 clean days of data.
stages.doneWhen: 20 sensors report every 10 minutes for 14 days in a row with fewer than 10% missing readings, and each site has a signed host OK.

roles.Leader: Wins host OK from CDAs and landowners
roles.Planner: Picks candidate and final sites
roles.Expert: Pulls flood history and maps who must approve sites
roles.Maker: Builds and installs the gauges
roles.Checker: Reviews the plan and checks 14 days of readings
roles.Storyteller: Collects residents' flood stories to show where water comes first
roles.User: Marks where their street floods

stages.name: Alerts
stages.goal: Text alerts reach 10,000 phones
stages.plainWords: Families sign up by text.
tracks: Write alerts in Yoruba, Pidgin and English
Set up short code, sender ID and opt-in
stages.why: Readings only matter when they reach a phone in a language people trust.
stages.howItFits: Expert writes alerts → Maker wires thresholds to the SMS gateway → Storyteller and Users fill the list → Checker proves test alerts arrive fast.
stages.doneWhen: 10,000 unique opted-in numbers; a test alert reaches 95% of 200 sampled phones within 5 minutes.

roles.Expert: Writes and tests alert text in three languages
roles.Maker: Builds the threshold rules and SMS pipeline
roles.Checker: Measures delivery time on test alerts
roles.Storyteller: Runs sign-up drives at markets and churches
roles.Patron: Funds a season of SMS credit
roles.User: Signs up and gets neighbours to sign up

stages.name: Test
stages.goal: Alerts arrive 2 hours before floods
stages.plainWords: Prove it warns people in time.
tracks: Log every flood with time water hit the street mark
stages.why: Only real floods prove the warning time.
stages.howItFits: Users timestamp the water → Checker computes lead time → Expert tunes thresholds → Maker keeps sensors alive → Leader decides what changes.
stages.doneWhen: At least 5 logged flood events; in 4 of 5 at Ogun River sites, the alert came 2 or more hours before water reached the street mark, backed by timestamped photos.

roles.Leader: Runs the after-flood review
roles.Expert: Re-tunes thresholds
roles.Maker: Repairs failed sensors within 48 hours
roles.Checker: Compares alert times with flood photos
roles.User: Photographs the street mark when water arrives

stages.name: Hand over
stages.goal: The local council runs it
stages.plainWords: Someone local keeps it going.
tracks: Sign handover with funding for 12 months
stages.why: Projects that never get handed over die when the money ends.
stages.howItFits: Storyteller writes the manual → Maker trains technicians → Checker confirms they can fix faults alone → Patron funds the reserve → Leader signs.
stages.doneWhen: Signed agreement between the LCDA environment unit and the CDA; 2 technicians each fix a sensor fault alone; 12 months of SIM and SMS costs in a joint account.

roles.Leader: Negotiates and signs the handover
roles.Maker: Trains local technicians
roles.Checker: Watches technicians fix a fault alone
roles.Storyteller: Writes the plain manual in English and Yoruba

strategies.name: Sensors + text alerts
strategies.bet: Cheap river sensors that text families when water rises fast.
strategies.sampleBlocker: Plan waits for the creator's OK
howItWorks: Map where water comes first on OpenStreetMap, from residents' pins and 10 years of flood records
Build ESP32 gauges and publish the full design, so any maker space can copy and repair them
Mount 20 gauges above the record flood line, each with its street's OK
Publish every 10-minute reading as open data and tune each site's alarm level after every real flood
strategies.rolesNeeded: 1 Maker (electronics), 1 Expert (hydrology), 1 Leader with CDA contacts
strategies.relations: Aims only at the Sensors checkpoint. River Marks races it to a working warning without electronics; its open readings would make River Marks' alarms earlier. Street Watch carries its alerts the last 100 metres.
strategies.strengths: Femi knows SMS systems from telecom work and lives on a street that floods. Open hardware at about $380 a gauge, and open readings anyone can check.

sample.teachingPoint: The mission creator OKs each new plan

detail.problem: Every rainy season (April to October) parts of Lagos flood. Families in Ogun River communities like Isheri North often learn the water is coming only when it reaches the door. National outlooks name Lagos as high-risk every year, but they work at the scale of a whole LGA and a whole season, not a street on a given night. Nigeria's 2012 floods killed about 360 people nationally, and the 2022 floods killed more than 600.
detail.whoItHelps: About 10,000 households (roughly 40,000 people) along the lower Ogun River (Isheri North, Ikosi-Isheri) and one flood-prone Lagos canal, starting in Kosofe and Ikosi-Isheri areas.
detail.whyUnsolved: Gauges get installed by projects and then stop working when the grant ends: batteries die, SIMs expire, sensors get stolen. Alerts need a trusted local sender and the right language, and nobody owns the cost of SMS after launch. Upstream dam-release information is not shared in a form residents can act on.
winning: 20 sensors (14 water-level, 6 rain) online with at least 90% uptime for a full rainy month
10,000 phones opted in by SMS keyword, with at least 60% choosing Yoruba or Pidgin
In 4 of 5 real flood events at the Ogun River sites, alerts arrived 2 or more hours before water reached the marked street level
False alarms make up fewer than 1 in 4 alerts over the season
A signed handover with 12 months of SIM, SMS and repair costs funded, and 2 trained local technicians
hardParts: Setting thresholds. Too low and people ignore the alerts. Too high and the warning arrives too late. Every site needs its own threshold, tuned against real events.
Keeping sensors alive through a rainy season: solar panels shaded by roofs, enclosures flooding, cables cut, theft.
Bulk SMS in Nigeria needs a registered sender ID and has to deal with Do-Not-Disturb filtering. Alerts that arrive late or not at all are worse than no alerts.
Ogun River levels depend on Oyan Dam releases upstream. Without release information, the gauge alone gives less warning.
Getting a local body to take over the running costs after the mission ends.
partners: A residents' Community Development Association that hosts sensors and owns the handover (Isheri Riverside CDA, fictional)
A maker space that builds and repairs gauges (Yaba Hardware Lab, fictional)
A licensed bulk-SMS aggregator with a registered short code (TextWave Nigeria, fictional)
A university hydrology group that checks thresholds (Lagoon Hydrology Group, fictional)
dataTools: NIHSA Annual Flood Outlook (Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency), yearly
NiMet Seasonal Climate Prediction
GloFAS (Copernicus Global Flood Awareness System) river forecasts
OpenStreetMap waterways and buildings; Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Tasking Manager
Common Alerting Protocol (CAP 1.2, OASIS) for alert messages
NCC rules on bulk SMS sender IDs and Do-Not-Disturb (2442)
Open hardware: ESP32 board, JSN-SR04T ultrasonic or radar level sensor, tipping-bucket rain gauge, 2G/4G modem, solar panel
detail.timeline: About 14 to 18 months: build and install before the April rains, run a full rainy season (April to October), then hand over. The slowest step is stage 3, because you have to wait for real floods to test against.

budget.Item: 20 sensor kits (gauge, board, modem, solar, enclosure)

budget.Note: Roughly 150,000 messages; price per SMS varies

budget.Item: Short code, sender ID and server

risks.Impact: Gaps in coverage on flood nights
risks.What we do about it: Host-watched sites, plain enclosures, spares stock

risks.Risk: SMS delayed or blocked by DND filtering
risks.What we do about it: Registered sender ID, transactional route, delivery-time tests, WhatsApp backup
Rate-of-rise rules, mid-season threshold tuning
No river visits when water is high or after dark; always two people
Involve the CDA from stage 1; fund a reserve

chats.text: Our gauge design is now public: parts list, code and the box. Any maker space can build one for about $380.
New plan in: painted depth marks plus phone photos, aiming straight at the council handover. No electronics to steal.
I like it, but who sends a photo at 2 a.m. in a storm? That's when Isheri floods.
Fair. That's why we add the free river forecast and dam-release news. Photos tune the alarm; they don't carry it alone.
Whatever wins, my captains carry it the last 100 metres. 6 streets have a captain now. We need 20.
Test run: the bot read 46 of 50 mark photos right. The 4 misses were blurry night shots.
Still waiting for the creator's OK on our plan. Anyone near Isheri North free to check 3 bridge sites on Saturday?
I'll come. Daylight only, and we stay off the riverbank.
First prototype has run on my roof for 9 days. Battery never dropped below 60%.
Problem: the ultrasonic sensor reads heavy rain as water. Testing a radar sensor next. It costs $25 more.
One captain wants a loudspeaker. Who knows a cheap one that runs on batteries?
Found 3 battery loudspeakers under $30 for sale in Lagos. List sent to your phone.
Painted the first 4 marks near the Isheri bridge. Yellow band every 25 cm, numbers you can read from 20 metres.
Paint fades in full sun. Road paint or metal plates?
Metal plates on the 10 most important sites, paint for the rest. Plates are $12 each.
Lined up 10 years of free river forecasts with 31 floods people remember. The forecast warned a day ahead for 19 of them.

title: Atlanta renters get the repairs they're owed
pitch: Atlanta renters live with broken heat and lose deposits because a lawyer costs too much. Build free, lawyer-checked open letters that any renter, tenant group or city can copy and improve.
rules: Legal information, not legal advice. Every letter and the tool say so, and anything involving a court date is sent to legal aid.
No letter goes live without a written sign-off from a Georgia-licensed lawyer, and it is re-checked whenever the law changes.
Renters' names, addresses and landlord details stay on their device by default. Nothing is sold or shared.
Calm, factual tone. Letters cite the law and the facts. No threats the law does not support.
Fair to landlords: letters ask for what the law gives, nothing more.
seedNotice: Illustrative workbook mission. People, progress, prizes, and outcomes shown as examples are not verified live activity.

detail.problem: Atlanta renters with a broken AC, a missing deposit or a sudden rent notice often don't know what Georgia law says, or how to put it in writing. A clear, dated letter is the paper trail that matters later in magistrate court, but most tenants never send one. Fulton County has one of the highest eviction filing rates in the US, with tens of thousands of filings a year.
detail.whoItHelps: Renters in Atlanta and the wider Fulton and DeKalb counties, starting with 1,000 households. Many are low-income and do not have a lawyer.
detail.whyUnsolved: Legal aid groups have long waiting lists and cannot write a letter for every repair dispute. Generic online templates ignore Georgia rules, and a non-lawyer giving individual advice risks the unauthorized practice of law. Keeping templates current as Georgia law changes (as with the 2024 Safe at Home Act) costs money that nobody pays for.
winning: 500 repairs made or deposits returned
10 letters, each signed off in writing by a Georgia-licensed lawyer, in English and Spanish
Each letter readable at a 6th to 8th grade level (tested with 5 renters per letter)
1,000 renters create a letter within 6 months of launch
At a 60-day follow-up, at least 35% of surveyed senders report a result (repair done, deposit returned, written notice received)
Zero personal data kept after the letter is made, unless the renter opts in to follow-up
hardParts: Staying on the right side of unauthorized practice of law: the tool can help renters fill in templates, but it cannot tell a specific person what to do.
Georgia has few tenant statutes and a lot of case law. Repair-and-deduct and rent withholding are risky, and a bad template can get a tenant evicted.
Deadlines: 30 days for deposit return, 7 days to answer a dispossessory affidavit. A letter sent at the wrong moment can do harm.
Small landlords (10 or fewer units, self-managed) are exempt from some deposit rules, so one deposit letter does not fit everyone.
Getting volunteer lawyers to commit and stay. Pro bono hours are scarce.
partners: A legal aid clinic that takes referrals for court cases (Peachtree Tenant Law Clinic, fictional)
Volunteer Georgia-licensed lawyers who sign off letters (Southside Pro Bono Circle, fictional)
A tenant union that tests letters and spreads the tool (Westside Renters United, fictional)
dataTools: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-13 (landlord's duty to repair) and § 44-7-14 (landlord liability for failing to repair)
O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-30 to 44-7-37 (security deposits; § 44-7-34 30-day return; § 44-7-35 penalties; § 44-7-33 move-in damage list)
Georgia Safe at Home Act, HB 404 (2024): fit-for-habitation duty, deposit cap, 3-business-day notice before filing for non-payment
O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50 et seq. (dispossessory proceedings; 7 days to answer)
O.C.G.A. § 44-7-24 (retaliation) and § 44-7-19 (rent control preemption)
Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f) (reasonable accommodation)
Georgia Landlord Tenant Handbook (Georgia Dept. of Community Affairs)
Eviction Lab data and Fulton County Magistrate Court public filing records (counts only)
City of Atlanta 311 / code enforcement complaints
detail.timeline: About 7 to 9 months. The slowest step is stage 2, lawyer sign-off, because volunteer lawyers review in their spare time and every letter can go through 2 or 3 rounds.

risks.Risk: A letter is read as individual legal advice
risks.What we do about it: Templates only, lawyer sign-off, clear disclaimer, referral for court matters

risks.Risk: A letter triggers retaliation or a filing
risks.What we do about it: Instructions explain § 44-7-24 and when to get help first
Two lawyers, small batches, honoraria
Yearly review after the Georgia legislative session, plus a reserve
Data stays on the device; no server storage by default

facts.Fact: A Georgia landlord must return the security deposit, or give an itemised list of deductions, within 30 days after the tenant moves out.
A tenant served with a dispossessory affidavit has 7 days to answer in magistrate court.
Georgia law preempts local rent control.
A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant for complaining about repairs to the landlord or to code enforcement.
The Safe at Home Act (2024) added a fit-for-habitation duty, capped deposits at 2 months' rent, and required a 3-business-day notice before filing for non-payment.
A landlord who wrongfully keeps a deposit can owe up to 3 times the amount withheld, plus attorney's fees.
Fulton County's eviction filing rate is among the highest of large US counties.

detail.problem: On hot summer days people in Berlin can't easily find free drinking water. Many of the city's roughly 2,000 historic street hand pumps are broken or missing from maps. Drinking fountains are spread across 12 districts and are switched off in winter, and no single public map showed which ones actually worked.
detail.whoItHelps: Berliners and visitors, especially older people, cyclists, homeless people and kids on hot days, across all 12 districts.
detail.whyUnsolved: Responsibility is split: drinking fountains have one operator, street pumps belong to the districts and the emergency water system. No one owned a citywide, up-to-date list of what works. Broken-pump reports landed in different inboxes, with no proof of where the pump was or what was wrong.
winning: 1,100 or more water points mapped in OpenStreetMap with photo and working status
300 or more broken points reported to the responsible office with a photo and exact location
200 or more reported points confirmed fixed by a re-visit
Data open under ODbL and live in common map apps
hardParts: Telling apart drinking fountains, ornamental fountains and hand pumps, which need different OSM tags and different offices.
Duplicate and outdated points already in OSM.
Getting reports to the right office in each of 12 districts.
Proving a fix: it needs a second visit, often weeks later.

EU Drinking Water Directive (EU) 2020/2184, Art. 16 (access to water in public places)
detail.timeline: 7 months, March to September. The slowest step was stage 3: districts took 4 to 12 weeks to fix pumps, and every fix needed a re-visit.

finished.What worked: Small one-hour squares, one standard report format, and dated photos as the only proof.
finished.What didn't: Outer districts lagged until bonuses came in. One district ignored single reports until we switched to a weekly spreadsheet. 90 reported points were still waiting when the season ended.
finished.Lessons:

• Find out how each office wants reports before sending any.

detail.problem: A single step at a front door, shop or clinic can shut out a wheelchair user completely. Ready-made portable ramps often cost $100–300 or more, which is out of reach for many families and small shops. WHO estimates about 80 million people need a wheelchair, and many live in homes with at least one step.
detail.whoItHelps: Wheelchair users, older people with walkers, and parents with prams. Builders were in 12 countries, including Germany, Kenya, India, Brazil, the Philippines and Mexico. It helps most where there is one step or a raised doorway.
detail.whyUnsolved: Ramps are cheap to make but costly to sell, because shipping, liability and markup add up. Open designs online were rarely load-tested, gave no cutting plan for local sheet sizes, or broke the slope rules. Nobody earns money from a free design, so nobody paid for the testing.

title: Water within reach in Barmer
pitch: When the village hand pump breaks, women in Barmer walk far for water. Build an open, photo-checked list of every pump in four blocks, so anyone can push for repairs and check they last.

sample.teachingPoint: Impact on the ground in India

detail.problem: In the Thar desert villages and dhanis (scattered hamlets) of Barmer, many families still rely on India Mark II hand pumps on deep borewells. When one breaks, women walk farther or buy tanker water. Repairs are the job of the Public Health Engineering Department (PHED), but broken pumps often go unreported or sit in a queue. We checked 2,600 pumps in 4 blocks and found 412 broken.
detail.whoItHelps: Households in about 180 villages and dhanis across 4 Barmer blocks. Under the old planning norm of 1 hand pump per 250 people, the 412 broken pumps were meant to serve tens of thousands of people.
detail.whyUnsolved: Official records count pumps installed, not pumps working, so nobody knows which ones are broken today. Mechanics cover huge distances with few vehicles and fix only what is reported. Panchayats have Finance Commission grants for drinking water but rarely spend them on hand pumps. Some failures are dry or saline borewells that no repair can fix.
winning: All 2,600 hand pumps in the 4 blocks checked, with a photo, GPS and a 20-stroke flow test
Every broken pump reported to PHED or Rajasthan Sampark, with a complaint number
300 pumps repaired within 6 months, each proven by a flow test
Fixed pumps re-checked 30 days later, and failures re-reported
Dry or saline borewells formally logged for a new bore or closure
hardParts: Distance and heat: dhanis are kilometres apart on sand tracks, and summer temperatures pass 45°C.

Diagnosis: a pump that gives no water could have a worn cup washer (an easy fix), a broken rod or rising main (needs parts) or a dry borewell (no repair will help). Volunteers must record symptoms, not guess.
Spare parts: rising-main pipes and cylinders run short, so repairs needing parts wait weeks.
Matching records: PHED pump IDs are often missing or painted over, so our list and theirs don't match.
Re-breaks: pumps with heavy use break again within weeks unless a village caretaker is trained and stocked.
partners: Village women's self-help groups who know every pump (Thar Mahila Mandal, fictional)
A local mechanics' cooperative that trained village caretakers (Marudhar Pump Sahayak, fictional)
A Barmer volunteer network for transport and phones (Desert Seva Network, fictional)
dataTools: PHED Rajasthan hand-pump records (obtained from block offices and via RTI)
Rajasthan Sampark portal and the 181 helpline, for complaints
Jal Jeevan Mission IMIS dashboard, for village tap coverage
15th Finance Commission tied-grant guidelines (drinking water and sanitation)
e-GramSwaraj, for panchayat development plans and spending
India Mark II deep-well hand pump specification (BIS)
ODK Collect / KoboToolbox, for the offline survey
RTI Act 2005 Sec. 6
detail.timeline: 7 months in total: 1 month to set up, 1 month to survey, 4 months of reporting and repairs, and a final month of re-checks. The slowest step was repairs that needed rising-main pipes, which waited weeks for stock.

budget.Note: Training only; repairs paid by PHED and panchayats

risks.What we do about it: No surveying from noon to 4 pm, work in pairs, carry water. Two volunteers got mild heat exhaustion in month 2, so survey hours moved earlier.
Hand-delivered with signed receipts, weekly check-ins, Sampark complaints in parallel. One block was slow until a monthly block meeting raised it.
Panchayats funded 40 repairs from tied grants; about 60 were still waiting at the end.

risks.Impact: About 50 pumps can never be repaired
risks.What we do about it: Logged separately for a new bore or closure, so they don't block the fix count.
GPS plus photo matching; PHED IDs painted on where missing.

facts.Fact: Rajasthan covers about 10% of India's land but has only about 1% of its surface water.
Jal Jeevan Mission, launched in 2019, aims to give every rural home a functional tap connection.
60% of the 15th Finance Commission's rural local-body grants are tied to drinking water and sanitation.
Older rural water-supply norms planned 1 hand pump or stand-post per 250 people.
facts.Source: Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme guidelines

facts.Fact: The India Mark II is India's standard deep-well hand pump and is common in Rajasthan.
facts.Source: BIS standard for the India Mark II deep-well hand pump

facts.Fact: Before the 2023 split that created Balotra district, Barmer was one of India's largest districts, at about 28,000 km².
facts.Source: Census of India 2011; Government of Rajasthan 2023

detail.problem: Crowded classrooms with closed windows build up stale air quickly. CO2 is a simple sign of that: outdoor air is about 420 ppm, and classrooms often climb past 1,000–1,500 ppm during lessons. Teachers can't feel it happening. Good CO2 meters cost $100 or more, which is too much for most schools to buy one per room.
detail.whoItHelps: Teachers and pupils in ordinary state schools, starting with 10 pilot classrooms. The plan was to reach about 200 classrooms if the price held.
detail.whyUnsolved: Accurate CO2 sensing needs an infrared (NDIR) sensor, and that part alone costs more than the whole $20 target in small batches. Cheap chips that claim to read CO2 actually estimate it from other gases and can be very wrong. Schools rarely have a budget line for air monitoring.
winning: Sensor reads within ±100 ppm (plus a few %) of a reference meter from 400 to 2,000 ppm
Full parts and build cost of $20 or less per unit at a 50-unit batch
A teacher can read it at a glance (green/amber/red) without an app
50 units running in 10 classrooms for 4 weeks
hardParts: Cost versus accuracy: cheap 'eCO2' chips are inaccurate, and accurate NDIR sensors are expensive.
Calibration: NDIR sensors drift and need a fresh-air baseline. Classrooms are rarely empty long enough for automatic calibration.
Small batches cost more per unit: cases, boards and shipping are priced for volumes of 1,000 or more.
Teachers need a simple signal, not a graph.
partners: A school in Milan that hosted the pilot (Scuola Primaria Navigli, fictional)
A maker space that lent a reference CO2 meter and a soldering bench (Officina Lambro, fictional)

finished.What happened: Sensors cost $90, not $20. The squad stopped at stage 2. $9,400 unspent went back to 61 funders. Work already approved was still paid.
finished.Timeline:
• Month 1: Squad formed; 3 sensors tested side by side. The $5 eCO2 chip failed badly.
• Month 2: 5 NDIR prototypes built; all passed ±100 ppm.
• Month 3: Real quotes for 50 units came in at about $90 each.
• Month 4: Audit confirmed $90. 4 trial units ran in 2 classrooms, and teachers liked the traffic light. Squad voted to stop; $9,400 refunded.
• Stage 3 (200 classrooms) never started.
finished.What worked: Testing accuracy before cost caught a sensor that would have misled teachers. The stop rule worked: approved work was paid and unspent money went back.
finished.What didn't: The $20 target was set before getting real quotes. The NDIR sensor alone costs more than $20 in small batches.
finished.Lessons:
• Get real batch quotes for the most expensive part before setting a price goal.
• 'eCO2' is not CO2. Check what a sensor actually measures.
• Set price goals as a range and tie them to volume.
• A clean stop with refunds builds trust for the next mission.

chats.text: Looking back: we stopped because 50 sensors would cost $90 each, not $20. The unspent $9,400 went back to all 61 funders.
The $5 eCO2 chip looked fine in an empty room and was badly wrong in a full one. Switching to NDIR made it honest, and much more expensive.
We ran 4 trial units in 2 classrooms. The kids loved the traffic light. When it went red they opened the window on their own. That part worked.
My mistake: we set the $20 goal before asking for real 50-unit quotes. Quotes came in month 3. Ask first next time.
The board design, firmware and all 48-hour test logs are now public. Anyone can build one or try to make it cheaper.
Final numbers: $18,000 raised, $8,600 paid for approved work, $9,400 refunded.
Two other teachers asked if they can borrow our 4 units. We're passing them on, not throwing them away.
If a new team can get NDIR sensors under $10 at volume, this mission is worth restarting. Everything we learned is waiting.
